title: Baseline Performance and the 72-Hour Performance Window Following Plyometric Withdrawal in Collegiate Sprinters.
abstract: Plyometric studies emphasise pre-post change, but coaches need to know what remains after the block ends. This single-cohort study followed 26 collegiate sprinters through 12 weeks of Monday plyometric training and 4 weeks of withdrawal, without a parallel control group. During intervention, 30 m sprint time and arm-assisted countermovement jump (CMJ) height were measured at 0, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h; 0 and 72 h were retained during withdrawal. Mixed models showed large week effects for sprint, F(1, 1534) = 2272.01, partial η2 = 0.597, 95% CI [0.570, 0.622], and CMJ, F(1, 1534) = 2537.82, partial η2 = 0.623, 95% CI [0.598, 0.647]. Time-point effects were evident, but week × time-point interactions were not. Relative to 0 h, sprint was 0.0098 s slower at 24 h and 0.0057 s faster at 72 h; CMJ was 0.311 cm lower at 24 h and 0.245 cm higher at 72 h (all Tukey-adjusted p < 0.001). Linear, quadratic, and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models were compared by rolling one-step error. ARIMA had the lowest rolling errors and provided exploratory, model-based references for weeks 13-16. During withdrawal, 1/4 sprint and 0/4 CMJ 0 h observations fell within the 95% prediction interval; mean absolute deviations were 0.0233 s and 0.794 cm. Three of four 72 - 0 h observations were within the interval for both outcomes. The 72 - 0 h series more often fell within their model-based intervals than the 0 h series, indicating different short-term patterns.

title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

title: Creatine supplementation in soccer players: a systematic review.
abstract:
AIM: Soccer places repeated demands on short-duration, high-intensity performance, including sprints, accelerations, jumps, and technical actions performed over the course of a match. Because these efforts depend heavily on rapid adenosine triphosphate (ATP) resynthesis, creatine is a plausible ergogenic aid for soccer players. However, findings in soccer-specific studies have been inconsistent, and previous reviews have addressed narrower questions using smaller evidence sets. This systematic review therefore examined the effects of creatine supplementation on performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes in soccer players.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 15 May 2025 in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. We included controlled clinical trials of creatine supplementation in male or female soccer players of any age or competitive level when an eligible placebo, control, or comparison condition was available. Outcomes were grouped into performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue domains. Domains from the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2) and the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool were used to produce study-level methodological summaries rather than formal result-specific risk-of-bias assessments. Because the studies differed substantially in design, supplementation protocols, populations, and outcomes, findings were synthesised qualitatively rather than pooled in a meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Source-level verification left 45 eligible reports representing 41 unique studies: 28 randomised parallel-group studies, 2 randomised crossover/repeated-condition studies, and 11 non-randomised or allocation-unverifiable controlled studies. Some trials reported favourable findings for repeated-sprint performance, anaerobic power, and muscular strength, but the comparative evidence was inconsistent and the certainty of evidence was very low. Findings for vertical jump performance and technical skills were mixed, while change-of-direction and endurance outcomes showed no consistent benefit. Recovery- and fatigue-related findings were also largely null or inconsistent. Body mass often increased, particularly after loading protocols, whereas evidence for gains in lean mass was limited and inconsistent.
CONCLUSION: The soccer-specific evidence for creatine supplementation remains suggestive rather than conclusive. Favourable findings have been reported for some repeated-sprint, anaerobic-power, and strength outcomes, but the comparative evidence is heterogeneous, often limited by unclear or nonsignificant between-group effects, and of very low certainty. Firm conclusions about efficacy are therefore not possible. Body mass commonly increased, especially after loading protocols, while effects on lean mass, endurance, change-of-direction ability, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes remain uncertain.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: The Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer: proposal for an ultrasound-based muscle injury classification.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To propose a novel ultrasound-based classification system for muscle injuries in soccer players, termed the Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer (SOMICS), and to evaluate its association, ordinal consistency, and agreement with the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a cross-sectional observational study including 51 adolescent male soccer players (11-19 years of age) with suspected acute myotendinous injuries. All athletes underwent ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 h after injury. Four experienced radiologists, working independently, reviewed the images.
RESULTS: Interobserver agreement was substantial for ultrasound (κ = 0.65) and MRI (κ = 0.70). A strong ordinal correlation was observed between SOMICS and BAMIC categories (ρ = 0.80; p < 0.001), with a statistically significant association (χ2 = 52.53; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The SOMICS demonstrated significant association, ordinal consistency, and substantial agreement with the BAMIC for severity stratification of muscle injuries. Although not intended to replace MRI-based classifications for prognostic decision-making, the SOMICS provides a structured, reproducible ultrasound-based approach that may be useful in clinical settings where MRI is not readily available or as a first-line imaging tool.
authors: Claudio Henrique Ivo de Araújo Ribeiro

title: Radial pressure wave treatment accelerates recovery from immobilization-induced soleus muscle atrophy and improves ankle range of motion in mice.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Disuse muscle atrophy following immobilization is characterized by decreased muscle mass and reduced joint range of motion (ROM). Radial pressure wave (RPW) treatment is a non-invasive modality that delivers mechanical energy to musculoskeletal tissues, but its efficacy in skeletal muscle recovery from disuse atrophy remains largely unknown. We examined whether RPW treatment accelerates soleus muscle structural recovery and passive ankle dorsiflexion ROM following immobilization-induced atrophy in mice. Furthermore, we investigated the underlying molecular signaling cascades and gene expression profiles associated with RPW-mediated recovery.

Soleus muscle mass, fiber cross-sectional area (CSA), and passive ankle dorsiflexion ROM were assessed. Gene set enrichment analysis revealed suppression of the forkhead box O (FoxO) signaling pathway and enrichment of the extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling pathway. title: Running-based rehabilitation does not improve muscle function after volumetric muscle loss despite improving hindlimb weight-bearing asymmetry in mice.
abstract: Volumetric muscle loss (VML) is a traumatic skeletal muscle injury characterized by chronic functional impairments in the affected muscle and adjacent uninjured bone. Rehabilitative strategies aimed at restoring limb function following VML, including voluntary running, have shown limited efficacy and in some cases have been detrimental. One potential explanation is disproportional loading of the uninjured contralateral limb during running, but evaluation of unilateral weight-bearing following VML has not been explored. This study was designed to evaluate if the limited response to rehabilitation following VML could be explained by limb loading asymmetry. Twelve-week-old C57Bl/6J mice (n = 24; equal males/females) were randomized to three groups: Naïve-Run, VML, and VML-Run. Two weeks post-VML, mice in running groups were provided free access to wheels for 6 weeks. Weight-bearing asymmetry was assessed before injury and biweekly thereafter. Terminally at ∼20 weeks of age, in vivo muscle function was evaluated, and muscles and bones were saved for analyses. Prior to injury, no difference in weight-bearing asymmetry was observed across groups. VML-injured mice exhibited similar weight-bearing asymmetries prior to running. Following 6 weeks of running, VML-Run mice regained weight-bearing symmetry comparable to Naïve-Run. Despite this, remaining muscle function remained persistently impaired following VML injury. Collectively this works suggests that voluntary running promotes favourable weight-bearing adaptations following VML, but does not improve muscle function or the mechanical properties of the adjacent bone.

title: Examining the Impact of Supramaximal Eccentric and Long-Lever Isometric Training Protocols on Isometric Hamstring Strength, Nordic Hamstring Performance, and Sprint Speed.
abstract: The aim of this study was to compare the effects of a 6-week higher-volume eccentric training protocol with a combined lower-volume eccentric and long-lever isometric protocol on posterior chain strength and sprint performance. Thirty-three NCAA Division II soccer players (men: n = 17, age = 19.7 ± 1.2 years, height = 178.9 ± 6.6 cm, body mass 79.8 ± 8.1 kg; women: n = 16, age = 20.1 ± 0.9 years, height = 166.7 ± 5.2 cm, body mass = 67.0 ± 12.1 kg) were allocated to either group via exhaustive minimization. Nordic hamstring exercise break-point angle (NBPA), rapid isometric hamstring strength (LLB), 20m sprint performance, and continuous angular knee extension velocity waveforms were assessed pre- and post-intervention, and following a 2-week detraining period. A significant main effect of time was observed for sprint, NBPA, and rapid isometric strength (p < 0.05); however, Bonferroni-corrected within-group comparisons reached significance only for sprint performance in both groups, with no significant between-group differences for any outcome. Equivalence testing supported comparable sprint adaptations between protocols but could not be established for eccentric or isometric hamstring strength. All discrete outcome measures were largely maintained or continued to develop following the detraining period though range-specific eccentric strength appeared more sensitive to the training cessation. A combined low-volume eccentric and isometric training approach may represent a viable alternative to higher-volume eccentric programming for hamstring strength and speed development, although this should be approached cautiously to preserve neuromuscular qualities relevant to hamstring injury risk mitigation.

title: Effectiveness of aerobic exercise on motor function and functional capacity in children and adolescents with neuromuscular diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the effectiveness of aerobic exercise, alone or combined with other modalities, on motor function and functional capacity in children and adolescents with neuromuscular diseases (NMDs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted (CRD420251110784). Five databases were searched up to September 2025. Randomized and non-randomized trials assessing aerobic exercise in children/adolescents with NMDs were included. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using RoB2, ROBINS-I, and GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated standardized mean differences (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI).
RESULTS: Eleven studies (227 participants) were included. Aerobic exercise showed no significant effect on motor function (SMD = 0.15, 95% CI: -0.10 to 0.40, I2=0%) but produced moderate improvements in functional capacity (SMD = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.99, I2=78%). Subgroup analyses suggested non-significant effects for sessions <40 min (SMD = 0.83) and combined aerobic plus strength training (SMD = 0.74). Sensitivity analyses showed one study disproportionately influenced results; excluding high-risk studies yielded SMD = 0.36 (I2=0%). GRADE indicated low certainty for motor function and very low certainty for functional capacity.
CONCLUSIONS: Aerobic exercise is safe and may improve functional capacity but not motor function in pediatric NMDs. Evidence is limited and needs for cautious interpretation and high-quality trials to inform clinical practice.

title: Acupuncture-Related interventions for exercise-induced delayed-onset muscle soreness in active adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis for sport rehabilitation.
abstract: BackgroundDelayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is a common post-exercise condition that can impair athletic performance, training quality, and rehabilitation.ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficacy and safety of acupuncture-related interventions for exercise-induced DOMS in active adults.MethodsPubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and CNKI were searched from inception to December 2025, with a manual reference-list update in January 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing acupuncture-related interventions with sham/placebo or no treatment in healthy adults with exercise-induced DOMS were eligible. Nine RCTs met the eligibility criteria, and seven contributed compatible pain data to meta-analysis. Two reviewers independently extracted data, assessed risk of bias using RoB 2, and rated evidence certainty with GRADE. Pain intensity on a 0-10 visual analogue scale was pooled using random-effects models.ResultsAcross seven RCTs, acupuncture-related interventions reduced DOMS pain at 24 h (MD -0.62, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.23), 48 h (MD -0.71, 95% CI -1.20 to -0.22), and 72 h (MD -0.84, 95% CI -1.35 to -0.32). Heterogeneity was low (I2 = 0%, 3%, and 23%, respectively). None of the pooled estimates reached commonly cited 1.0- or 1.3-point pain thresholds, and no DOMS-specific minimal clinically important difference has been established. Evidence certainty was moderate.ConclusionAcupuncture-related interventions may provide modest short-term reductions in DOMS pain, but their clinical importance remains uncertain. The evidence base is small and does not support dry-needling-specific conclusions. Larger, rigorously controlled, modality-specific RCTs are needed.
journal: Journal of back and musculoskeletal rehabilitation

title: The Potential Impact of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely prescribed for mood disorders. Their association with musculoskeletal side effects raises the question of potential SSRI impact on exercise-induced muscle damage and recovery.
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this prospective cohort study was to determine if SSRI use influences muscle function following a bout of eccentric exercise designed to induce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS).
METHODS: Subjects between 18 and 30 years of age were recruited in a university setting. This included 1 group taking SSRIs prescribed by their health care provider, and a control group not using SSRIs. Subjects performed a DOMS induction protocol consisting of 300 eccentric knee extensions on an isokinetic dynamometer. Muscle soreness, thigh circumference, quadriceps flexibility, and isometric quadriceps strength were measured at baseline and at 24-, 48-, 72-, and 96-hour post-DOMS protocol. Comparisons were made between SSRI users and control subjects.
RESULTS: Thirty-six subjects included 18 SSRI users and 18 controls. The DOMS protocol induced muscle soreness in both groups (P < .001 when compared with baseline). At 72 hours a between-group difference was observed for thigh muscle flexibility (MD = 11.2, SE = 5.0, 95% CI [0.9, 21.4], P = .033, ηp2 = .126) but no additional significant between-group differences in soreness, strength, thigh circumference, or flexibility were noted at any timepoint.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this population, SSRI use had no effect on muscle soreness, circumference, or strength of the quadriceps following eccentric DOMS-inducing exercise. A difference in flexibility between SSRI and control groups at a single time point likely reflects a Type 1 error and is not likely of clinical consequence. These findings suggest SSRIs do not impair short-term recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in healthy young adults, but potential SSRI impacts on longer-term training adaptations and recovery in athletic populations remain unknown.

title: Effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate on exercise-induced biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation in federated road cyclists.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined the effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate (CPH) on biomarkers associated with exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation in federated male road cyclists.
METHODS: Twenty-four participants completed a 14-day intervention receiving either 12 g/day of chickpea protein hydrolysate (EXP) or a placebo (PLA) following training sessions. The selected dose was based on previous studies demonstrating antioxidant and immunomodulatory bioactive properties of the hydrolysate. Nutritional intake and training were registered. Body composition and biochemical markers of muscle damage and inflammation were assessed before and after the study.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in body composition, training load, or dietary intake between groups, indicating controlled experimental conditions. However, between-group analyses of change scores revealed significant differences for lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; p = 0.04) and C-reactive protein (CRP; p = 0.02), favoring the experimental group. LDH decreased in the EXP group while increasing slightly in the placebo group, whereas CRP decreased in EXP and increased in PLA. Although creatine kinase (CK) showed a favorable pattern in the EXP group, the between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.062). Myoglobin followed a similar downward trend. The high baseline protein intake (>2 g/kg/day) and short intervention duration may have limited changes in body composition, nevertheless, the observed biomarker responses suggest that CPH supplementation may influence selected physiological processes associated with exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress.
CONCLUSIONS: In trained cyclists with high habitual protein intakes, 14 days of CPH supplementation did not alter body composition but was associated with favorable changes in selected biomarkers related to exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress compared with placebo. Given the short intervention period and the absence of direct assessments of recovery or performance, these findings should be interpreted as short-term biochemical responses. Further studies are required to determine their physiological relevance and whether these biomarker changes translate into meaningful improvements in recovery, training adaptation, or athletic performance.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: The content and reporting completeness of physical therapist-led interventions for glenohumeral osteoarthritis: a systematic review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study synthesised the content and reporting completeness of published physical therapist-led interventions for glenohumeral osteoarthritis (GHOA).
METHODS: This systematic review undertook electronic database searches in PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane, CINAHL and PEDro (until June 2025) for any peer-reviewed articles/studies describing physical therapist-led interventions across non-surgical and perioperative settings for adults aged 45 years and over with GHOA. The content and reporting completeness were synthesized using the 22-item Template for Intervention Description and Replication for rehabilitation interventions (TIDIeR_Rehab).
RESULTS: Overall, 134 articles/studies describing 156 physical therapist-led interventions were included, comprising mostly case series designs (n=47, 35.1%) or narrative reviews (n=38, 28.4%). Of the remaining 49 articles/studies, only 11 were studies reporting RCT results and three were protocols of RCTs in progress. Intervention content varied considerably, and the overall completeness of intervention item reporting was poor (only 18%). Interventions in non-surgical contexts commonly included strengthening exercises (n=33, 53.2%), range of motion (ROM) exercises (n=23, 37.1%), and electrotherapy modalities (n=16, 25.8%). Sling immobilisation was most reported in postoperative interventions (n=64, 72.7%). Many different proposed mechanisms of action were reported (n=49, 31.4%); but all were biomechanically orientated.
CONCLUSION: Very few high-quality empirical studies evaluating physical therapist-led interventions for GHOA have been published. We found substantial heterogeneity in the content of published physical therapist-led interventions, and the reporting completeness was generally poor. This suggests considerable uncertainty regarding best practice physical therapy for GHOA in terms of intervention content. Future high-quality empirical research is needed, preferably using RCT designs that include clear descriptions of interventions.

title: Effects of anti-aging diets and exercise on age-related musculoskeletal diseases via gut microbiota modulation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This review summarizes evidence on how anti-aging diets and exercise influence age-related musculoskeletal diseases through modulation of the gut microbiota. With population aging, these diseases are public health concerns. The gut microbiota regulates bone, joint, and muscle health via the gut‑joint, gut‑bone, and gut‑muscle axis. Few reviews integrate diet-exercise synergy with mechanistic pathways linking microbial changes to tissue outcomes.
DISCUSSION: Anti‑aging dietary strategies, classified into caloric restriction (ketogenic diet, fasting‑mimicking diet, intermittent fasting, time‑restricted feeding) and isocaloric nutrient restriction (e.g. protein or amino acid restriction), reshape gut microbiota composition and function. Caloric restriction and intermittent fasting reduce inflammation and benefit joint and muscle health, whereas long‑term ketogenic or protein/amino acid restriction may adversely affect bone density and muscle anabolism. Moderate exercise increases microbial diversity, enriches beneficial taxa (Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium), and boosts short‑chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, especially butyrate. Exercise also strengthens intestinal barrier integrity, reduces lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑induced systemic inflammation, and alleviates osteoarthritis (OA), bone loss, and sarcopenia in preclinical models. Combined diet and exercise may provide greater benefits than either alone. However, most evidence derives from animal or small human studies, and causality remains unclear. Future research should clarify causal mechanisms via multi‑omics and germ‑free models.
CONCLUSION: This review suggests that both anti-aging diets and moderate exercise may improve age-related musculoskeletal diseases partly through gut microbiota modulation. Given substantial inter‑individual variability, future research should prioritize personalized nutrition and exercise prescriptions tailored to microbiota, genetic background, and lifestyle. These findings inform precision strategies to promote healthy aging.

title: Culturally Embedded Participation Restrictions in Indian Adults With Knee Osteoarthritis: An ICF-Based Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify culturally relevant functioning issues experienced by Indian adults with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured focus group interviews was conducted with 38 ambulatory adults (35-85 years) diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Participants were recruited from physiotherapy outpatient departments and community settings using maximum variation sampling. Interviews were conducted in Gujarati, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Meaningful concepts were systematically linked to ICF categories using established linking rules. Dual independent coding and consensus discussions ensured the analytic rigour.
RESULTS: This study included 38 participants with KOA. Fifty-five meaningful second-level categories were identified. The most represented components were activities and participation (41.2%) and body functions (29.4%). Frequently mapped first-level categories included mobility (n = 22), neuromusculoskeletal and movement-related functions (n = 9), d6 domestic life (n = 10), community, social and civic life (n = 7) and products and technology (n = 9). Sixteen additional categories not represented in the existing ICF Core Set for OA emerged, particularly relating to culturally embedded activities such as floor sitting, squatting for toileting and religious participation. Environmental barriers, including inaccessible infrastructure and limited rehabilitation services, influenced disability experience.
CONCLUSION: Functioning among Indian adults with KOA is influenced by culturally embedded participation demands and contextual barriers that are insufficiently captured in the existing ICF Core Set for osteoarthritis (OA). These findings provide preliminary empirical support for contextual validation of the ICF Core Set for OA and inform potential culturally responsive adaptation for KOA.

title: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation.
METHODS: This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening.
RESULTS: Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

title: Anatomic feasibility of using Shark Screw tendon for humeral ligament re-construction in medial and posterolateral elbow instability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medial and posterolateral rotational instability of the elbow, often resulting from collateral ligament insufficiency, can lead to pain and functional impairment. Surgical re-construction is indicated when conservative treatment fails, yet complications such as graft failure and donor-site morbidity persist. This study investigates the anatomic and biomechanical feasibility of the Shark Screw tendon as a representative human allogeneic bone screw for humeral ligament fixation in cases of elbow instability.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen cadaveric specimens were used to evaluate the feasibility of the use of a Shark Screw tendon for humeral fixation on both medial and lateral sides. Cyclic loading and failure testing were performed to assess time-zero fixation characteristics and failure load.
RESULTS: A total of sixteen testing scenarios were conducted on the specimens. Implantation was technically feasible without anatomic limitations related to implant size or positioning. Six graft failures occurred (38%), all attributable to poor tissue quality. Tendon slippage was observed in 9 of 16 cases (56%) under progressively increasing axial load, while the Shark Screw tendon remained seated. The mean failure load was 101 N (±50) for medial insertions, 118 N (±77) for lateral insertions, and 110 N (±64) overall. After 100 cycles, tendon displacement averaged 1.1 mm (±0.4) during extension-flexion on the medial side, 1.0 mm (±1.0) on the lateral side, and 1.0 mm (±0.7) overall. During supination-pronation, displacement was 0.8 mm (±0.7) medially, 1.0 mm (±0.8) laterally, and 0.9 mm (±0.7) overall. No anchor pullout was observed, although one anchor tip fractured during insertion.
CONCLUSION: The Shark Screw tendon appears to be a feasible biologically integrative alternative for humeral fixation in medial and posterolateral elbow ligament re-construction, demonstrating preliminary time-zero fixation characteristics in a cadaveric model. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes.

title: Nonoperative Management of an Acute Complete Achilles Tendon Rupture With Mesenchymal Stem Cells and Extracellular Vesicles: A Case Report.
abstract: An acute complete rupture of the Achilles tendon with a large intertendinous gap is conventionally regarded as a surgical indication, yet operative repair carries a significant burden on wound-healing and potential for neurovascular complications, whereas nonoperative care may be limited by re-rupture and incomplete functional recovery. Human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (hUC-MSCs) and their secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) exert immunomodulatory, pro-angiogenic and pro-tenogenic paracrine effects that could support tendon healing. A healthy 45-year-old recreationally active male sustained an acute complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon while playing tennis. A 3.0-T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a full-thickness mid-substance rupture located 6.1 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion, with a 3.7 cm gap. He delayed treatment and opted out of surgical management and was offered nonoperative care with a combined biologic regimen: two ultrasound-guided intralesional injections of hUC-MSC-derived EVs (a total of 30 × 10⁹ vesicles) deposited into the tendon gap, both stumps, and the peritendon along with three consecutive daily intravenous (IV) infusions of hUC-MSCs (approximately 1.7 × 10⁶ cells/kg of total body weight) as a paracrine priming adjuvant, alongside an injury-guided functional rehabilitation program. Pain measured using the numeric rating scale (NRS) decreased from 10/10 at baseline to 0/10 at six months post-intervention. At final follow-up (approx 14 months) the patient had returned to regular weight training and jogging without pain or functional limitations. On physical examination, the Thompson Test was negative, the Achilles Tendon Total Rupture Score (ATRS) and the American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) ankle-hindfoot scores were both calculated as 100/100, and instrumented biomechanical testing showed near-symmetric lower-limb range of motion and balance. Follow-up MRI demonstrated a remodeled tendon with restoration of continuity and no residual gap. No mild or severe adverse events were reported during or after procedures. In this single case report, a combined regimen of systemic hUC-MSCs and intralesional hUC-MSC-derived EVs was associated with imaging-confirmed tendon healing and full functional recovery of an acute complete Achilles tendon rupture managed nonoperatively. This treatment protocol serves as a hypothesis-generating observation with potential for validation in controlled prospective studies.

title: Molecular drivers of intercellular communication in physical exercise: insights from omics approaches.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Physical activity enhances overall health by promoting coordinated communication among organs. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) play a key role in this process by transporting proteins, RNAs, lipids and other molecules that reflect how different tissues respond to physiological stress. Proteomics has been instrumental in clarifying how exercise reshapes EVs, providing insights into their role in mediating intercellular communication and systemic adaptations.
AREAS COVERED: Current proteomics of exercise-induced EV remodeling are overviewed and integrated with complementary transcriptomic and lipidomic findings. We highlight modality-dependent changes in EV abundance and cargo, including antioxidant enzymes, metabolic regulators and muscle-associated markers, such as α-sarcoglycan. Methodological challenges in EV isolation, molecular profiling, data normalization, and functional validation are critically examined, along with the potential of EVs as minimally invasive sources of biomarkers and therapeutic vectors.
EXPERT OPINION: Circulating EVs transmit information between tissues to support the body's adaptation to exercise. Proteomics has identified important molecular signatures in EVs, but significant gaps remain regarding their cellular origin, the influence of exercise modalities on cargo selection, and the functional roles of these vesicles. Progress will require standardized workflows and integrated multi-omics approaches, combined with functional assays and physiological parameters of exercise adaptation.

title: Cartilage-targeting engineered probiotic bacterial extracellular vesicles treat osteoarthritis through modulation of matrix homeostasis.
abstract: Reversing extracellular matrix (ECM) metabolic dysregulation to facilitate cartilage repair represents a key therapeutic strategy for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment. Owing to the avascular nature of joint structures, intra-articular injection is a commonly used clinical administration route. However, the current drug retention time is insufficient to effectively reverse OA progression. In this study, we demonstrated that natural bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are capable of repairing cartilage damage. We modified Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)-derived BEVs with a chondrocyte-targeting peptide to prolong their therapeutic efficacy. Engineered BEVs, as a drug delivery system, are capable of continuously transporting endogenous miRNAs. Cartilage-targeting LGG-EVs (W-LGG-EVs) penetrate deeply into cartilage tissue and promote extracellular matrix secretion by chondrocytes. Furthermore, W-LGG-EVs were shown to restore cartilage homeostasis and ultimately alleviate stress-related OA. BEVs, as a novel and safe therapeutic agent, hold clinical feasibility.

title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.

title: DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel reprograms the immuno-oxidative microenvironment to support stem cell-based cartilage repair in osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent degenerative joint disease, and stem cell therapy is often limited by a hostile joint microenvironment. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) and damage-associated cell-free DNA (cfDNA) cooperatively drive innate immune activation, inflammatory macrophage polarization, and chondrogenic instability, forming an immuno-oxidative barrier to cartilage repair. Here, we developed a bioactive DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel (MNKB/HA) to remodel this niche and enhance BMSC-mediated cartilage repair. MNKB/HA integrates Mn3O4 nanozymes with Kartogenin (KGN)-engineered bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) in an injectable hyaluronic acid matrix. Mn3O4 exhibited SOD- and CAT-like activities, scavenging O2·-, H2O2, and ·OH, while efficiently adsorbing cfDNA and CpG-ODN to suppress TLR9/MyD88 signaling and M1 polarization and promote M2 polarization. In vitro, 10 μg/mL Mn3O4 was cytocompatible, protected BMSCs and chondrocytes from H2O2-induced apoptosis, and reshaped inflammatory secretion, with IL-10 increased 8.3-fold and TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β reduced. KGN stabilized the chondrogenic phenotype (SOX9, COL Ⅱ, ACAN), while its combination with Mn3O4 synergistically enhanced chondrogenic stability under oxidative/inflammatory stress. In rat OA, intra-articular MNKB/HA reduced OARSI scores, restored COL II and ACAN, decreased MMP13, improved subchondral bone microarchitecture, and attenuated synovitis and osteophytes. MNKB/HA also reduced synovial cfDNA, weakened TLR9 signaling, promoted M2 polarization, and showed intra-articular retention for at least 10 days without notable systemic toxicity. Thus, MNKB/HA remodels the immuno-oxidative niche through synergistic ROS scavenging and cfDNA adsorption, providing a strategy for stem cell-mediated cartilage repair in OA.

title: Perineural Release with or Without Balloon Decompression for the Treatment of Lumbosacral Discogenic Syndromes in Professional Athletes.
abstract: Background: Lumbosacral discogenic syndrome (LSDS) is a common cause of low back pain (LBP) and lower limb pain (LLP) in athletes, often resulting in impaired sporting performance and delayed return to sport (RTS). Evidence regarding minimally invasive interventions, such as epidural perineural release (PNR), remains limited in athletic populations. Aim: This study aimed to compare outcomes following PNR with versus without balloon decompression neuroplasty in athletes with LSDS. Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of PNR performed between 2019 and 2024 for the treatment of LSDS among professional athletes. Demographic, clinical, and outcome data were collected from medical records and follow-up assessments. Pain intensity was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), while patient-reported outcomes were evaluated using the EuroQoL-5D (EQ-5D). Additional outcomes included pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations, and self-reported health scores. Results: A total of 33 patients who had one intervention were included. Significant improvements were observed in all pain, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes following treatment (all p < 0.001). Maximum, minimum, and average pain intensity decreased from 7.5 ± 1.7 to 2.8 ± 2.2, 3.8 ± 2.3 to 0.3 ± 0.7, and 5.6 ± 1.7 to 1.5 ± 1.2, respectively. All EQ-5D domains and quality of sleep also improved significantly (all p < 0.001). Pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations increased significantly, from 24.8 ± 23.2 to 49.7 ± 26.7 min, 18.4 ± 20.0 to 44.1 ± 23.1 min, and 25.5 ± 23.7 to 44.6 ± 24.9 min, respectively (all p < 0.001). Self-reported health scores improved from 51.9 ± 22.6 to 83.0 ± 14.3 (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Epidural perineural release, with or without balloon decompression neuroplasty, was associated by significant improvements in pain, functional capacity, and quality of life among athletes with LSDS refractory to conservative management. These findings suggest that PNR may be a promising minimally invasive treatment option; however, controlled prospective studies are required to establish its effectiveness and determine the additional benefit of balloon decompression.

title: Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness.
abstract: Optimizing astronaut mission readiness is a multidisciplinary endeavor that should integrate concepts from aerospace medicine, human performance, sports science, nutrition, and engineering. Situating astronauts within a theoretical framework similar to that of operational athletes, while addressing top human systems capability needs outlined for future missions, may be optimal for promoting sustained health and performance before, during, and after missions to low-Earth orbit, the lunar surface, and Mars. Mission readiness can be optimized by enhancing physiological and behavioral/psychological performance through data-driven and individualized exercise countermeasures, health and performance monitoring, precision nutrition, and rehabilitation strategies. Appropriate and stable space food systems that facilitate adequate provision of nutrients and fluids to prime astronauts for mission-critical tasks and operational demands are needed, though research is needed into potential nutritional considerations that might be useful for future missions. Behavioral readiness programs should emphasize stress inoculation, adaptive decision-making, communication, Earth-independent operation functionality, conflict resolution, leadership, and team-based problem-solving before flight to promote healthy team dynamics in-flight, along with proper society reintegration and uptake of family and occupational roles post-flight. Exercise remains an essential countermeasure during spaceflight, with an emphasis on maximizing fitness before launch to mitigate in-flight declines and on maintaining fitness levels and functionality during flight through high-intensity multimodal exercise. Following return to Earth, rehabilitative programs serve to restore cardiovascular, sensorimotor, and skeletal function, followed by enhancing skill-based performance components through a phase-based training program. Continuous monitoring systems that provide insight into health, performance, sleep, cognitive, nutritional, and recovery status should enable data-driven decision-making on physical readiness across all mission phases. By integrating insight from multiple disciplines, this unifying approach delivers a theoretical framework for sustaining astronaut health and performance during extended-duration missions.

title: Sleep-timing irregularity moderates the within-participant association between training load and next-morning heart rate variability in university sport participants: a 28-day study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heart rate variability (HRV) describes beat-to-beat variation in cardiac intervals; the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) is a time-domain index of short-term cardiac vagal modulation. We examined whether nightly deviation from habitual sleep midpoint moderated the association between prior-day internal training load and next-morning natural-log-transformed RMSSD (lnRMSSD), and whether analogous interactions were present for resting heart rate, wellness strain, and countermovement-jump (CMJ) height.
METHODS: University students engaged in regular sport training completed 28 days of habitual monitoring. Internal load was session duration multiplied by session rating of perceived exertion. Wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries estimated sleep midpoint, and 5-min morning RR recordings yielded lnRMSSD. Mixed models separated within- and between-participant components and tested within-participant load (per 100 arbitrary units [AU]) × absolute midpoint deviation (per 30 min).
RESULTS: The analysis included 1,232 mornings from 54 participants (57.4% female; age 21.0 ± 1.7 years). At each participant's mean midpoint deviation, greater-than-usual load was associated with lower next-morning lnRMSSD (β = -0.0089, 95% CI -0.0127 to -0.0051; p < 0.001). At mean load, greater-than-usual midpoint deviation was also associated with lower lnRMSSD (β = -0.0156, 95% CI -0.0268 to -0.0045; p = 0.006). The interaction was negative (β = -0.0101, 95% CI -0.0153 to -0.0048; p < 0.001). Thus, the inverse within-participant association between load and lnRMSSD strengthened as sleep-timing irregularity increased. No load-by-midpoint interaction was detected for resting heart rate, wellness strain, or CMJ height after false discovery rate adjustment. The primary interaction persisted after adjustment for prior-morning lnRMSSD (β = -0.0096, 95% CI -0.0147 to -0.0046; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The within-participant association between training load and next-morning cardiac vagal modulation was moderated by sleep-timing irregularity. These field-based associations do not establish a sleep mechanism, causal recovery effect, or decision threshold.

title: Music-based emotional regulation and nutrition strategies for mental health support among medical student-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medical student-athletes face combined academic, clinical, and competitive training demands that may disrupt sleep, dietary routines, emotional regulation, recovery, and cognitive functioning.
OBJECTIVE: To examine associations between naturally occurring music-based emotional regulation, self-selected nutrition routines, psychophysiological recovery, and mental health-related markers using a non-interventional multimodal digital phenotyping framework.
METHODS: Over 8 weeks, 120 medical student-athletes were monitored without prescribed music, diet, therapy, or behavioral intervention. Data included wearable-derived nocturnal heart-rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep-wake rhythm, activity and training load, participant-recorded music use, meal timing, hydration routines, food-photo logs, and brief emotional reflections. Three indices were constructed: The Music Regulation Pattern Index, Nutrition Rhythm Stability Index, and Psychophysiological Recovery Balance Index.
RESULTS: Monitoring feasibility was high and index reliability was acceptable. Music-regulation patterns were more strongly associated with emotional balance and focus-related language, whereas nutrition-rhythm stability was more closely associated with sleep regularity, heart-rate variability stability, and recovery balance.
CONCLUSION: Naturally occurring music-use and nutrition-rhythm behaviors showed distinct associations with emotional and physiological recovery markers. Multimodal digital phenotyping may help identify potentially protective lifestyle patterns in medical student-athletes while preserving an observational, non-causal interpretation and avoiding unsupported treatment claims.

title: The effect of macular carotenoids and omega-3 supplementation on performance in precision sports: the sport nutrition intervention in performance exercise (SNIPE) study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Macular carotenoids improve visual performance in healthy individuals, but these benefits have yet to be tested on athletes. The SNIPE study examined how the macular carotenoids [lutein (L), zeaxanthin (Z), meso-zeaxanthin (MZ)] with omega-3 fatty acids (ω3) impact visual functions and sports performance in precision sports.
METHODS: In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 67 athletes and players randomly received either an active supplement containing L, Z, MZ + ω3 (the formulation), or a placebo containing sunflower oil over a 9 month period. Key measurements included blood serum L, Z and MZ concentrations, skin carotenoid score (SCS), visual acuity (VA) and contrast sensitivity (CS), subjective visual function, sleep health (SH), and sport specific performance tests during simulated competitions.
RESULTS: Results showed that the active group, compared to placebo, exhibited statistically significant improvements in L (88%), Z (107%), MZ (0 to 0.226 μmol/L) blood concentrations, SCS (25%), CS at 6 cpd during dim condition (p = 0.008, η2 = 0.141), and SH in archery (p = 0.023, η2 = 0.242) and Egame (p = 0.041, η2 = 0.237). Sports performance also improved for the active group, including total shooting score of 60 shots (p = 0.047, η2 = 0.081) for shooters and archers, and simple motor time (p = 0.018, η2 = 0.302) and a suggestive trend toward faster choice reaction time (p = 0.054, η2 = 0.213) for Egame players, when compared to the placebo group.
CONCLUSION: The study provides novel evidence that supplementing with carotenoids and omega-3 fatty acids enhances visual function and sports performance in precision sport athletes and players. Further research should attempt to identify the exact mechanisms by which these nutrients are enhancing visual function. These findings highlight the opportunity to add these complementary bioactive nutrients of the eye and brain to athletes' diets to help achieve peak performance in sports.

title: Strategic Application of Post-exercise Cold-Water Immersion to Enhance Performance Recovery and Adaptation: An Umbrella Review of 15 Published Systematic Reviews with Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletes commonly implement post-exercise cold-water immersion (CWI), with several meta-analyses having assessed its effectiveness.
OBJECTIVES: To thoroughly review, appraise, and summarise existing systematic reviews with meta-analyses (SRMA) examining the effects of post-exercise CWI on the recovery of exercise performance and adaptation.
METHODS: An umbrella review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines. Methodological quality was assessed using AMSTAR 2, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. PROSPERO registration: (CRD420251103267). Eight databases were searched, including Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Embase, MEDLINE, and PubMed. Systematic reviews with meta-analyses of peer-reviewed randomised controlled trials examining post-exercise CWI vs passive rest or other recovery modalities on performance, training adaptation, or physiological, biochemical, and perceptual outcomes in healthy humans were included, with restriction to the English language.
RESULTS: Fifteen SRMAs published between 2011 and 2025, comprising 161 unique studies, were included. Overall methodological quality was low to critically low, and certainty of evidence was low to very low, mainly due to inconsistency and imprecision. Protocols of 10-15 min at 10-15 or 5-10 °C appear to be most effective for improving performance and recovery. Post-exercise CWI resulted in significant improvements in muscular power at 24 h post-high-intensity exercise and at 24-48 h post-eccentric exercise, and in jump performance at 24-48 h, despite impaired jump performance in the initial hours after post-exercise CWI. Endurance performance improved immediately after CWI, but CWI produced no later benefits or positive effects on adaptations. CWI did not improve muscular strength performance, and impaired strength and hypertrophic gains. CWI improved heart rate variability immediately after exercise, reduced muscle soreness up to 96 h, and lowered creatine kinase (CK) concentrations between 24 and 72 h, with no significant effects on C-reactive protein or interleukin-6 up to 72 h. No immediate impact on blood lactate or lactate dehydrogenase was found, although some reductions appear 24-72 h post-exercise.
CONCLUSIONS: Post-exercise CWI confers outcome-specific recovery benefits but may impair resistance training adaptations with chronic use. These findings support a periodised, context-driven approach to CWI implementation rather than routine application after all exercise sessions.

title: Feasibility and Preliminary Effects of AI-Generated Personalized Sleep Feedback in High School Female Soccer Players: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep supports mood regulation and injury prevention in high school female athletes; however, insufficient sleep is common in this population. Wearable devices enable continuous assessment of objective sleep metrics, but personalized feedback based on daily sleep data remains underexplored.
OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated the technical and operational feasibility of a multicomponent AI-supported mobile health (mHealth) intervention that delivered personalized sleep feedback to high school female soccer players. Sleep efficiency was the primary preliminary efficacy outcome; other sleep-related measures were secondary or exploratory outcomes, and mood state and sports injury severity were exploratory outcomes.
METHODS: We conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial among 25 high school female soccer players from a single team. The study briefing and system setup began on August 18, 2025, and the trial was retrospectively registered with the University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN) Clinical Trials Registry on April 7, 2026 (UMIN000061189). Weeks 1 to 4 constituted the baseline period. After the week 5 baseline questionnaires, participants were stratified by median baseline total sleep time (TST) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score and randomly allocated 1:1 to the intervention (n=12) or control (n=13) group. During weeks 6 to 9, the intervention group received GPT-4o-generated personalized feedback via LINE on days with valid prior-night Fitbit data, whereas the control group received daily nonpersonalized sleep information. Technical and operational feasibility outcomes included message delivery success, valid Fitbit wear nights, questionnaire completion, technical problems, adverse events, and privacy breaches. Secondary outcomes included TST, wake after sleep onset (WASO), subjective sleep quality, sleep difficulty, and daytime sleepiness. Deep, light, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep durations, mood state, and sports injury severity were exploratory outcomes.
RESULTS: All 25 participants completed the trial. Message delivery success and questionnaire completion were 100% in both groups. Median valid Fitbit wear nights were 26 (IQR 24-28) in the intervention group and 22 (IQR 15-26) in the control group. No major technical problems, adverse events, or privacy breaches occurred. Change in sleep efficiency, the primary preliminary efficacy outcome, favored the intervention group (Hodges-Lehmann between-group difference 2%, 95% CI 0.50%-4%; P=.046; r=0.35). Nominal between-group differences were also observed for the Japanese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI-J) total score and sleep difficulty score and, among exploratory outcomes, REM sleep duration and total mood disturbance. No between-group differences were observed in TST, WASO, deep or light sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, or sports injury severity.
CONCLUSIONS: The multicomponent AI-supported mHealth intervention demonstrated technical and operational feasibility in this single-team setting. Preliminary, hypothesis-generating between-group differences were observed in sleep efficiency and selected subjective sleep and mood outcomes. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence of established effectiveness and require confirmation in a sufficiently powered trial.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: UMIN Clinical Trials Registry UMIN000061189; https://tinyurl.com/tw3d7aku.

title: Persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain in young athletes: an overlooked biopsychosocial determinant of return to sport trajectories - a focused narrative review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain is common in young athletes, yet its role in recovery and return to sport (RTS) decision-making remains insufficiently acknowledged. In youth sport, pain is often normalized or viewed primarily through an injury-centered lens, despite its potential to shape function, participation patterns, and athletic trajectories over time.
AREAS COVERED: This focused narrative review aimed to (1) synthesize current evidence on persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain in young athletes and (2) propose a developmentally informed biopsychosocial framework for understanding its implications for RTS. Electronic searches were conducted in PubMed, PsycINFO, and SPORTDiscus for studies published from 1 January 2006, through 28 February 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking and targeted hand-searching of reference lists. It integrates evidence on definitions, prevalence, clinical presentation, psychosocial and contextual factors, functional interference, and RTS decision-making, conceptualizing ongoing pain as an overlooked determinant of RTS trajectories.
EXPERT OPINION/COMMENTARY: In young athletes, pain should not be treated as a peripheral symptom or addressed only when recovery is delayed. More informed RTS decisions require attention not only to physical recovery markers, but also to how pain is experienced, interpreted, and managed throughout recovery. A developmentally informed biopsychosocial perspective may support earlier recognition, safer return decisions, more stable participation, and better long-term health outcomes.

title: An Intensified Training Period Reduces REM Sleep but this Decline Can Be Mitigated by Ketone Ester Supplementation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We previously showed that a strenuous training day disrupts sleep efficiency and REM sleep, and that these disturbances can be counteracted by ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl-(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate (KE) supplementation. However, the impact of prolonged intensified training on sleep quality, as well as the potential modulating effect of KE are unknown.
METHODS: We performed a double-blind study in which twenty-four trained male athletes completed a 7-week training program with a gradual increase in training load while receiving either 25g of a control drink (CON, n=12) or 25g of KE (n=12) after each training session and 30 minutes before sleep. At the start (PRE), week 3 (MID), and the end (POST) of the training program, we evaluated sleep using polysomnography, and perceived stress/recovery balance using the REST-Q questionnaire. Timing, duration, and relative intensity of exercise on each testing day were identical.
RESULTS: The progressive increase in training load induced a decrease in the perceived stress-recovery state in both groups (PRE: 73±21 vs. POST: 40±37, p<0.001, Hedges' g = 1.097). From PRE to MID, sleep efficiency improved by 3% in both groups (p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.663) while wakefulness after sleep onset reduced by 2% (p=0.031, Hedges' g = 0.716). However, from PRE to POST, total REM sleep decreased by 2% in CON but increased by 3% in KE (p=0.002, for KE vs. CON, Hedges' g = 0.939). Perceived sleep quality did not differ between groups throughout the intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data indicate that KE supplementation did not enhance the beneficial effect of an initial increase in training load on sleep but prevented the decline in REM sleep upon a further training load increment.
journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis.
abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

title: More than fuel: Why athletes need better language around food.
abstract: "Food is fuel" is a widely used phrase in sport settings intended to emphasize the importance of nutrition for performance. While nutrition is essential for health and success, this framing may unintentionally reinforce a narrow, performance-oriented understanding of eating that has implications for athletes' relationships with food and their bodies. Athletes are at heightened risk for eating concerns, low energy availability, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), and aspects of sport culture may contribute to rigid, rule-based approaches to eating. This commentary argues that "food is fuel" language reflects and reinforced broader sports norms centered around optimization, control, and performance. Potential consequences include reduced attunement to internal cues and the moralization of food choices, particularly in sport environments where appearance and performance are closely intertwined. Language is proposed as a modifiable factor for prevention and more flexible, athlete-centered approaches to discussing food and eating are identified. Rather than dismissing the importance of nutrition in athletics, this commentary advocates for broader conceptualizations of eating that acknowledge its physical, psychological, social, and cultural functions and support athletes in developing sustainable relationships with food throughout and beyond their athletic careers.

title: Anti-inflammatory and early osteogenic potential of a 96% ethanol extract of Drynaria bonii.
abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Drynaria bonii H. Christ rhizome is traditionally used in Vietnamese medicine for fractures and musculoskeletal disorders. However, the effects of extraction solvent on chemical composition and biological activities relevant to the inflammatory and early mineralization phases of bone repair remain insufficiently defined.
AIM OF THE STUDY: This study compared 30%, 70%, and 96% ethanol extracts of D. bonii (DB30, DB70, and DB96, respectively) to identify a lead extract for further fracture-healing-oriented investigation.
METHODS: Rhizome extracts prepared with 30%, 70%, and 96% ethanol were profiled by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-QTOF-MS/MS). TNF-α inhibition was evaluated in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; acute anti-inflammatory activity was assessed in carrageenan-induced mouse paw edema; and calcium-associated staining was evaluated in canine mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) cultures using Alizarin Red S (ARS). Acute oral toxicity was assessed at 5000 mg/kg, and selected constituents were isolated from DB96. The four NMR-characterized constituents were subsequently evaluated by molecular docking against IκB kinase β (IKKβ).
RESULTS: The extracts showed distinct qualitative LC-MS/MS profiles, with DB70 displaying a broader curated phenolic/flavonoid profile and DB96 showing a different compositional pattern. DB96 produced the strongest TNF-α inhibition (IC50 = 32.05 μg/mL), compared with DB70 (63.73 μg/mL), whereas DB30 did not reach 50% inhibition at 100 μg/mL. DB96 also showed the largest numerical paw-edema inhibition among the extract groups at 1 and 24 h; however, statistical comparisons were performed only against the disease-control group and not among active treatment groups. In canine MSC cultures, DB96 at 50 μg/mL showed the highest descriptive normalized ARS-positive area among the extracts (12.0 ± 2.1%), although staining remained weak relative to the positive control and did not establish complete osteogenic differentiation. Betulin, ursolic acid, rutin, and kaempferol were isolated from DB96 and independently identified by NMR from a preparative DB96 batch. Among these constituents, ursolic acid and betulin showed the most favorable predicted IKKβ docking profiles, with binding energies of -8.52 and -8.41 kcal/mol, respectively. No mortality or overt acute toxicity was observed for any of the three extracts after a single oral dose of 5000 mg/kg.
CONCLUSION: The findings support DB96 as the lead extract among the three preparations for subsequent mechanistic and bone-repair-oriented investigation. Docking provided complementary mechanistic support for possible interactions of selected DB96 constituents with IKKβ, but did not establish direct target inhibition. Direct fracture-healing efficacy, definitive osteogenic differentiation, quantitative constituent enrichment, and repeated-dose safety remain to be established.

title: Cardiovascular Effects Associated with the Female Athlete Triad: Emerging Evidence Statement from the Female and Male Athlete Triad Coalition.
abstract: This is an emerging evidence statement from the Female and Male Athlete Triad Coalition. This paper complements the 2025 updates to the Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statements addressing the State of the Science and Clinical Guidelines for Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment and Return to Play. This paper examines emerging evidence of cardiovascular alterations in Triad-affected female athletes with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and functional hypothalamic oligomenorrhea, including vascular, hemodynamic, autonomic and lipid perturbations. The clinical significance of these surrogate markers of cardiovascular function and their long-term cardiovascular implications remain to be determined. Notwithstanding, the current work extends existing Triad frameworks by recognizing cardiovascular perturbations potentially associated with energy deficiency and hypoestrogenism as an important consideration in female athlete health. We outline an evidence-informed research framework, including longitudinal, dose-response, and multimodal assessments, to characterize the onset, magnitude, physiological significance, and reversibility of cardiovascular alterations in athletes with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and functional hypothalamic oligomenorrhea. By integrating evidence from sports physiology, endocrinology, and cardiovascular medicine, this state-of-the-science synthesis provides a roadmap for future research, screening, and intervention strategies. It also underscores the importance of evaluating cardiovascular health as a potential component of the broader physiological consequences of energy deficiency, alongside menstrual dysfunction, and impaired bone health.

title: Integrated physical, cognitive and psychological rehabilitation following multiple ACL reconstructions in a professional handball player: a case report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries with repeated surgical interventions and postoperative complications pose a major challenge in sports rehabilitation. Beyond neuromuscular deficits, psychological and cognitive readiness often remain impaired, increasing reinjury risk and threatening athletic careers. This case highlights an integrated rehabilitation strategy addressing physical, psychological, and cognitive domains in a professional athlete with a complex surgical history.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 31-year-old white Serbian male professional handball player with a history of two ACL reconstructions, meniscal repairs, a postoperative knee infection, and multiple arthroscopic interventions presented with persistent knee instability, pain, and psychological distress. Following repeated failed return-to-play attempts, he underwent a ten-week intervention combining therapeutic exercises, sports psychology sessions, and neurocognitive dual-task training. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included gait analysis, postural control, strength testing, ACL-specific functional tests, and psychological evaluations. Post-intervention assessments showed improvements in gait mechanics, postural stability, neuromuscular strength, and reduced functional asymmetries, alongside lower cognitive anxiety and greater motivation.
CONCLUSIONS: This case suggests that an interdisciplinary, multimodal rehabilitation approach, integrating physical, psychological, and cognitive strategies, may help address both physical deficits and psychological barriers in athletes with multiple ACL surgeries and complex postoperative courses. Such integration may support function, confidence, and readiness in high-performance athletes facing career-threatening injuries.

title: Dietary Supplement Use and Beliefs Among Athletes at the 2025 Canada Games.
abstract: Dietary supplement use is widespread among athletes; however, limited data exist regarding supplement use and beliefs among Canadian youth athletes. This cross-sectional online study aimed to examine dietary supplement use and related beliefs among athletes competing at the 2025 Canada Games in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. A total of 473 respondents participated in the survey. Of the 473 participants, 385 completed responses to the dietary supplement (DS) questions. Among participants who reported their sex, 125 were male and 189 were female. Overall, 36% of participants reported current dietary supplement use. Supplement use was significantly higher among males than females (47% vs. 23%, p < .001) and increased with age (p = .001). The most commonly reported supplements were protein powder (49%), sports drinks (46%), and creatine (45%). Primary reasons for use included maintaining good health (76%), increasing energy (54%), and promoting recovery (50%). Coaches (50%) and healthcare professionals (49%) were the most frequently reported information sources. Supplement users demonstrated significantly stronger positive beliefs regarding benefits of dietary supplements compared with non-users (all p < .001). Ordinal logistic regression showed that supplement users had greater odds of stronger agreement that supplements improve performance (OR = 5.50, 95% CI: 3.31-9.13, p < .001). These findings highlight the use of dietary supplements among Canadian youth athletes and support the need for targeted nutrition education to promote informed decision-making.
