title: Effects of acute Capsaicin analogue intake on athletic performance: a three-level meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Capsaicin analogues have been proposed as potential ergogenic aids, but their acute effects on athletic performance remain inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of acute capsaicin analogue intake on exercise performance using a three-level meta-analysis.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and the Cochrane Library were searched up to April 1, 2025. Randomized controlled trials examining acute oral capsaicin analogue intake in healthy adults were included. Outcomes were classified into strength, power, muscular endurance, and aerobic capacity. Hedges' g was calculated using a three-level random-effects model.
RESULTS: Twenty-one randomized crossover trials with 67 effect sizes were included. Acute capsaicin analogue intake significantly improved overall athletic performance compared with placebo (g = 0.20, 95% CI [0.07, 0.33], p < 0.01). Subgroup analyses showed significant effects on power (g = 0.39) and muscular endurance (g = 0.25), but not on strength or aerobic capacity. Phenylcapsaicin showed the largest effect, and benefits were more evident in trained participants. Dose-response analysis suggested a nonlinear pattern, with low-to-moderate doses showing more stable benefits.
CONCLUSIONS: Acute capsaicin analogue intake may produce small but significant improvements in athletic performance, particularly in power and muscular endurance. However, due to heterogeneity, publication bias, and very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.

title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Weight reduction before competition has long been a major challenge for combat-sports athletes. Unscientific weight-loss practices not only increase the risk of hormonal imbalance, electrolyte disturbance, and impaired immune function but also compromise athletic capacities such as aerobic and anaerobic performance and explosive power. This study investigated the potential benefits of tangeretin, a natural citrus extract, on athletic performance. These benefits include the regulation of hormone secretion, the optimization of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and the promotion of muscle synthesis and lipid utilization, which may help athletes reach their target weight.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the effects of tangeretin supplementation on body-composition and sports-performance indicators in female combat-sports athletes, and to evaluate its efficacy for simulated precompetition weight loss.
METHODS: Thirty female combat-sports athletes (4 wrestlers, 3 boxers, 9 sanda athletes, 3 judokas, and 11 taekwondo athletes) were recruited. A paired, randomized, double-blind design was used. All 30 participants were first paired according to sport and competitive level, then randomly allocated to either a tangeretin group or a placebo group (15 per group). The 30-day intervention comprised a double-blind nutritional supplement, a dietary questionnaire, blood sampling and analysis, body-composition assessment, isokinetic muscle-strength testing, and aerobic-capacity testing, to evaluate the effects of tangeretin (400 mg/day) on performance and health-related outcomes. These outcomes included body-composition indicators (e.g. body-fat percentage, fat mass, lean-body mass), fat-distribution indicators (e.g. limb and regional fat mass, gynoid fat mass), glucose and lipid-metabolism indicators (e.g. LDL-C, total cholesterol, free fatty acids), hormone indicators (e.g. cortisol, testosterone), muscle-strength indicators (e.g. peak torque of hip, knee, and ankle flexors and extensors), and maximal-oxygen-uptake-derived indicators (e.g. VO2max heart rate, time to exhaustion). Statistical significance was assessed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).
RESULTS: (1) Body weight: 80.0% of athletes in the tangeretin group lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% (5 athletes) reached their competition weight class. (2) Body fat: body-fat percentage in the tangeretin group decreased from 23.92 ± 0.87% to 22.92 ± 0.89%; trunk, upper-limb, lower-limb, and android-region fat mass decreased by 6.77%, 8.77%, 4.43%, and 8.09%, respectively. (3) Glucose and lipid metabolism: HDL-C increased by 8.86% (P = 0.002), whereas triglycerides decreased by 25.00% (P = 0.048). (4) Sports performance: peak torque during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension increased significantly in the tangeretin group. VO2max also improved from 42.80 ± 1.13 to 43.46 ± 1.32 ml/kg/min.
CONCLUSION: Tangeretin supplementation effectively reduced body weight and fat mass (both overall and regionally) in female combat-sports athletes. Among the participants, 80.0% lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% reached their competition weight class, indicating a strong effect on precompetition weight loss. Moreover, tangeretin improved aerobic capacity and lower-limb joint muscle strength, thereby enhancing competitive performance.

title: Photobiomodulation versus ischemic preconditioning for protection against exercise-induced muscle damage: protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) occurs after unaccustomed eccentric exercise and may impair muscle recovery. Preconditioning with photobiomodulation (PBM) or ischemic preconditioning (IPC) may mitigate EIMD; however, no study has directly compared their effectiveness. This study aims to compare the effects of PBM and IPC applied prior to eccentric exercise on indirect markers of EIMD and associated perceptual responses. We hypothesized that MVIC trajectories would differ among the PBM, IPC, and sham groups, with PBM expected to provide greater preservation of MVIC than IPC. A prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial with concealed allocation, blinded outcome assessors and statistician, and intention-to-treat analysis will be conducted. Healthy men (18-35 years) will be randomly allocated to PBM, IPC, or sham groups (n = 15 per group). After the intervention, participants will perform an eccentric exercise protocol for the elbow flexors consisting of 30 repetitions using a dumbbell load numerically matched to maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) values, with 45-second rest intervals. The primary outcome will be MVIC. Secondary outcomes include rate of force development, delayed-onset muscle soreness, pressure pain threshold, ultrasound echo intensity, range of motion, perceived exertion, and affective responses. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, immediately after exercise (only MVIC), and at 24-, 48-, and 72-hours post-exercise. The primary analysis will assess the group × time interaction on MVIC using linear mixed-effects models, while secondary outcomes will be analyzed exploratorily. This study will provide, to our knowledge, the first direct comparison between PBM and IPC as preconditioning strategies to attenuate EIMD. The findings may help determine the most effective and clinically applicable intervention by considering both physiological and perceptual responses, thereby supporting decision-making in clinical and sports settings.Trial registrationBrazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (REBEC), RBR-6gr5kf; registered February 19, 2020; amended August 26, 2026.

title: Calf Injuries: An Anatomy-Based Approach to Diagnosis, Management and Return to Sport.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Calf muscle injuries are common in athletes but represent a heterogeneous group of lesions involving different muscles and myoconnective structures. This review provides a practical overview of gastrocnemius-soleus injuries, with particular emphasis on how anatomical characterization can contribute to diagnosis, management and return-to-sport decision-making. It also examines the limitations of current evidence and the extent to which increasingly detailed imaging findings translate into clinically meaningful information.
RECENT FINDINGS: Advances in ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging have improved the identification of specific injury patterns involving the gastrocnemius and soleus. Recent studies support moving beyond a muscle-based diagnosis towards more precise characterisation of the myoconnective structures involved. However, evidence linking individual anatomical patterns to prognosis and return-to-sport outcomes remains limited and largely observational. Current rehabilitation approaches favour progressive, criteria-based loading rather than fixed timelines, while return-to-sport decisions increasingly integrate clinical recovery, functional capacity, sport-specific demands and acceptable risk. No validated calf-specific rehabilitation or return-to-sport criteria are currently available. Anatomical characterization provides a useful framework for understanding the heterogeneity of calf muscle injuries but should inform rather than determine clinical management. Rehabilitation should remain function-led and progressively restore the mechanical capacities required for sport, while return to sport should be considered a multifactorial decision rather than the result of isolated imaging findings, tests or predefined timelines. Future prospective studies should determine which anatomical features provide clinically relevant prognostic information and develop validated calf-specific functional and return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Muscle satellite cell dysfunction in critical illness: niche biology, regenerative failure, and implications for recovery.
abstract: Adult skeletal muscle can regenerate. After muscle injury, muscle stem cells (satellite cells) can generate new muscle fibers. Under normal conditions, satellite cells are mitotically quiescent and located beneath the basal lamina of muscle fibers. In response to regenerative stimuli, satellite cells activate and proliferate as myogenic precursor cells. After several rounds of cell division, these precursor cells differentiate and fuse to form new muscle fibers. A subset of proliferating myogenic precursor cells returns to a quiescent state to replenish the satellite cell pool through self-renewal. Intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) affects many critically ill patients partly due to acute muscle loss. It is a major physical component of post-intensive care syndrome. Current explanations of ICU-AW focus on rapid protein breakdown and impaired energy metabolism during the early catabolic phase, but these mechanisms do not fully explain why some survivors fail to rebuild muscle once the initial catabolic stress has subsided. In this review, we argue that persistent weakness may also reflect defective muscle regeneration, with satellite cell dysfunction and niche abnormalities as plausible contributors. Recent serial-biopsy studies suggest that dysfunction can occur without stem-cell depletion: satellite cell number can be preserved even when differentiation or later proliferative capacity is impaired in culture. We first review the normal satellite cell niche, including the parent fiber, microvasculature and perivascular cells, extracellular matrix, resident immune and interstitial cells, and systemic signals, with separate consideration of the diaphragm. We then examine how critical illness affects these compartments and how cell-intrinsic defects may additionally impair regeneration. We use this evidence to develop three working hypotheses (niche-detached activation, abortive myogenesis, and niche locking) and treat them as testable models rather than recognized mechanisms. Finally, we consider how future studies might measure, target, and test these processes.

title: Rehabilitation of Athletes With Hamstring Strain Injury: SONAFE-Brazil Clinical Practice Guideline.
abstract: SYNOPSIS: The National Society of Sports Physical Therapy (SONAFE-Brazil), the official organization representing sports physical therapists in Brazil, developed this clinical practice guideline to support clinicians and athletes in managing hamstring strain injury. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach was used to address the clinical question "Which interventions provided by physical therapists improve rehabilitation outcomes in athletes with hamstring strain injury?" The guideline provides an updated and targeted synthesis of evidence from randomized clinical trials, offering practical guidance to inform clinical decision making by physical therapists across diverse health care and sports settings. title: Heterologous contralateral repeated bout effect: eccentric knee extensor conditioning enhances neuromuscular fatigue resistance and attenuates muscle stiffness in contralateral elbow flexors in young women.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The repeated bout effect (RBE) protects skeletal muscles from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD). While homologous contralateral RBE is well-documented, the existence of heterologous RBE-specifically whether lower limb conditioning can protect upper limb muscles-remains debated.
PURPOSE: This study investigated whether high-intensity eccentric exercise of the knee extensors attenuates eccentric exercise-induced neuromuscular fatigue and muscle stiffness and preserves neuromuscular control in the contralateral elbow flexors.
METHODS: Twenty-four sedentary young women were randomized into a Knee Extensor-Contralateral Elbow Flexor (KE-CEF) group and a Control Elbow Flexor (CEF) group. The KE-CEF group performed 60 maximal eccentric contractions (MaxEc) of the non-dominant knee extensors, followed 14 days later by 30 MaxEc of the dominant elbow flexors. The CEF group performed only the elbow flexor MaxEc. Outcome measures, including maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVC), Acoustic Radiation Force Impulse (ARFI) imaging, and the Joint Release Angle (JRA) test, were assessed up to 120 h post-exercise.
RESULTS: The KE-CEF group demonstrated significantly less MVC loss immediately post-exercise compared to the CEF group (70.00 ± 19.85% vs. 57.67 ± 8.28%; p = 0.029). Furthermore, prior lower limb conditioning significantly attenuated peak muscle stiffness at 48 h (ARFI: 108.25 ± 4.73% vs. 125.63 ± 6.99% in CEF) and entirely preserved JRA proprioceptive stability during peak fatigue (26.58 ± 0.78° vs. 24.75 ± 1.55°; between-group p = 0.001).
CONCLUSION: These findings provide novel evidence that a single bout of lower limb eccentric exercise confers a robust heterologous protective effect on upper limb muscles, highlighting the role of global systemic and neural adaptations in cross-limb rehabilitation strategies.

title: Using High-Field Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy to Measure Muscle Glycogen in Patients With McArdle Disease.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION/AIMS: Patients with McArdle disease demonstrate exercise intolerance with muscle contractures and episodic rhabdomyolysis. Additionally, some patients show progressive fat replacement of paraspinal and shoulder muscles with aging. The cause of fat replacement in older McArdle patients is unknown but could relate to a higher glycogen accumulation in these muscles in line with what is found in Pompe disease. The aim of the study was to investigate if this is also the case in McArdle disease, which could imply that excess levels of glycogen accumulation are a potential driver of fat replacement of muscle.
METHODS: Using 7 Tesla 13C magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we measured glycogen noninvasively in lumbar, thigh, and calf muscles in 14 patients with McArdle disease and 19 healthy controls.
RESULTS: Patients with McArdle disease showed increased levels of glycogen in all muscles compared to controls; calf (3.2 times normal, p < 0.005), hamstrings (2.7 times normal, p < 0.005), anterior thigh compartment (2.7 times normal, p < 0.005), and lumbar muscle (2.1 times normal, p < 0.005). Glycogen was evenly distributed among muscle groups in both patients with McArdle disease and healthy controls.
DISCUSSION: Our results are in line with previous studies showing two to three times increased glycogen compared to control in muscle biopsies. We found no variability in glycogen concentration among muscles that could indicate glycogen as a predictor of muscle injury in McArdle disease.

title: Core Muscle Injury: A Combined Orthopaedic and General Surgery Algorithmic Approach for Diagnosis, Imaging, and Treatment.
abstract: » Core muscle injury (CMI) is a common cause of groin pain in athletes and reflects pathology of the inguinal canal, rectus abdominis-adductor longus (RA-AL) aponeurosis, and pubic symphysis. » There is a substantial lack of consensus on terminology and diagnostic criteria for CMI, hindering standardized evaluation, management, and research initiatives. » Diagnosis relies on structured history, physical examinations, and provocative maneuvers to identify CMI and concurrent pathology, and fluid-sensitive pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterize RA-AL injury. » Treatment strategies differ across sports medicine physicians, general surgeons, and orthopaedic surgeons, underscoring the need for early cross-departmental referrals to ensure all contributing pathologies are comprehensively identified and addressed. » When both adductor/RA-AL aponeurosis and inguinal canal/abdominal wall pathologies are present, prioritizing collaborative cases between orthopaedic and general surgeons is essential for decreasing operating room time, streamlining rehabilitation, and optimizing return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Quadriceps Strength Recovery Trajectories Associate with Pre-Operative Predictors but not Clinical Outcomes Following ACL Reconstruction.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Quadriceps weakness following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is common, however distinct longitudinal strength trajectories not have been examined. This study aimed to i) identify strength trajectories measured pre-operatively to 12 months post-ACLR, and determine associations with ii) pre-operative demographics, patient-reported outcomes (PROs: Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score [KOOS], Tegner, Marx) and ACLR concomitant surgeries, and iii) clinical outcomes post-ACLR including cartilage compositional changes (via magnetic resonance imaging [MRI] T1ρ relaxation times) and 12-month KOOS.
METHODS: Isometric quadriceps strength was measured bilaterally pre-operatively and at 4, 6, and 12 months. Group trajectory modeling characterized longitudinal strength recovery in ACLR and uninvolved limbs, which were combined to define dual-limb recovery patterns. Tibiofemoral and patellofemoral cartilage composition was measured pre-operatively and at 12 months post-ACLR. Dirichlet regressions examined associations between trajectories and demographics, surgeries, PROs, and cartilage changes.
RESULTS: 59 participants were included (58% female; age, 21.9 ± 4.7y; BMI, 24.55 ± 3.7kg/m 2). Three combined trajectories were identified: bilaterally weak (51%), which demonstrated uninvolved limb strength declines and failure to recover ACLR limb pre-operative strength; bilaterally strong (38%), which demonstrated minimal uninvolved limb declines and ACLR limb pre-operative strength recovery; and weak uninvolved, strong ACLR limb (12%). Lower pre-injury Tegner scores associated with bilaterally weak membership (p = 0.01), where probability increased from 0.27 (score of 10) to 0.61 (score of 0). Medial meniscectomy associated most with bilaterally weak membership (p<.001, 0.86 probability). No associations were found between trajectories and clinical outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: While individuals who failed to restore ACLR limb strength demonstrated bilateral quadriceps weakness pre-operatively, persons who demonstrated greater pre-operative bilateral strength recovered ACLR limb strength. Medial meniscectomy associated with an inability to restore quadriceps strength.

title: [L-lactylation regulatory network in orthopedic degenerative diseases].
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To explore the therapeutic potential of L-lactylation in degenerative disc disease, arthritis, muscle degeneration, exercise metabolism, and osteoporosis.
METHODS: Literatures about L-lactylation in metabolic regulation, inflammatory response, and bone homeostasis at home and abroad in recent years were extensively reviewed. Emphasis was placed on analyzing the molecular regulatory networks of L-lactylation and its related clinical therapeutic potential in intervertebral disc degenerative diseases, arthritis, muscle degeneration and exercise metabolism, and osteoporosis.
RESULTS: L-lactylation reprograms metabolic flux by modifying key enzymes, and regulates chromatin dynamics through histone/non-histone modifications, thereby modulating macrophage polarization, osteoclast-osteoblast balance, and extracellular matrix remodeling. In intervertebral disc degeneration, tumor necrosis factor α activates glycolytic enzymes to promote L-lactylation, while glutamine supplementation reduces L-lactylation levels and activates the adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase catalytic subunit α pathway; hypoxia inducible factor 1α promotes the extracellular transport of L-lactylation by upregulating monocarboxylate transporter 4. In osteoarthritis, lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) overexpression leads to elevated histone L-lactylation levels, which in turn upregulates the transcriptional activity of triosephosphate isomerase 1 and accelerates cartilage degradation. In rheumatoid arthritis, artemisinin induces L-lactylation of pyruvate kinase M2 and inhibits the proliferation and migration of fibroblast-like synoviocytes. In tendinopathy, L-lactylation exerts regulatory effects in the aspects of extracellular matrix, immunity, nerves and blood vessels. In osteoporosis, L-lactylation affects osteogenic differentiation and bone resorption through regulatory axes such as Forkhead box F1, crystallin alpha B/ferritin heavy chain 1, and JunB, and interventions including LDHA regulation and scopolamine administration can promote osteogenic differentiation.
CONCLUSION: L-lactylation plays a dual regulatory role in orthopedic degenerative diseases, and its spatiotemporal dynamics and tissue specificity provide new opportunities for precise treatment. Although target specificity and clinical validation still face challenges, targeting L-lactylation modification is expected to become a new direction for disease-modifying therapy of orthopedic degenerative diseases.

title: A Practical Pipeline for Patient-Specific Musculoskeletal Modeling: A Comprehensive MRI-Based Framework.
abstract: Patient-specific musculoskeletal (MS) modeling can provide estimates of internal joint loading that canot be measured directly. However, limitations in automated segmentation due to data-scarce environments, morphing difficulty caused by anatomical variability, and functional non-alignment are major bottlenecks that hinder the practical application of modeling and reduce productivity in musculoskeletal research. To comprehensively address these practical issues, this study proposes and validates an integrated, automated modeling framework.. First, we automatically segmented the lower extremity bones of the 4 knee osteoarthritis patients using a multi-atlas-based segmentation algorithm. By integrating the segmented bone with motion capture and force plate data, a modeling pipeline including multi-stage morphing and functional alignment processes was implemented. Using the constructed customized model, the medial and lateral knee contact forces (FMC and FLC) were estimated during a single-leg step-up exercise, and these were compared and evaluated against the results based on manual segmentation. The contact forces estimated through the automated segmentation framework demonstrated high consistency with the manual results. The mean absolute error ranged from 0.04 ± 0.03 to 0.06 ± 0.03 BW for FMC, and from 0.06 ± 0.04 to 0.09 ± 0.07 BW for FLC, and the intraclass correlation coefficient demonstrated a high correlation of over 0.99 across all patients. This study demonstrated that the proposed automated pipeline provides a practical approach to address misalignment caused by anatomical variability, while generating joint load estimates equivalent to the manual approach. By addressing key methodological challenges, this study will bring patient-specific models closer to future clinical application, where they could help assess individual loading across different activities and inform treatment and rehabilitation strategies.

title: Aerobic Exercise Ameliorates Osteoarthritic Chondrocyte Degradation in Osteoarthritis via Regulating E2F8/NLRP14 Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Although physical activity is known to mitigate disease risks, its protective molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. E2F8, a regulator of cell cycle and metabolism, showed significant differential expression between osteoarthritis (OA) and exercise models, suggesting it may link mechanical activity to OA alleviation. In vitro, Interleukin-1 Beta (IL-1β) simulated inflammation. In vivo, OA was induced in rats via Monosodium iodoacetate (MIA) injection. The effects of E2F8 and mechanical stress were assessed using moderate treadmill exercise, histology, and joint observation. Bioinformatic analysis, cyclic tensile strain, Western blot, immunofluorescence, and gene knockdown were used to investigate mechanisms. In OA rats, E2F8 was downregulated in cartilage while NLRP14 increased. Exercise reversed E2F8 downregulation, alleviated cartilage degeneration, restored anabolic activity, and reduced inflammatory catabolism linked to senescence. In vitro, mechanical stress reversed the IL-1β-induced anabolic/catabolic imbalance by regulating the E2F8/NLRP14, mitigating OA progression. Mechanical stress enhances E2F8 expression in osteoarthritic chondrocytes, which in turn protects cartilage by suppressing the expression of NLRP14. These findings underscore the role of E2F8 as a mechano-sensitive mediator and highlight the potential of exercise or exercise-mimetic therapies as effective strategies for preventing and treating OA.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology

title: [Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with double-bundle artificial ligament based on four-dimensional impingement free mechanism: a comparative study with single-bundle reconstruction].
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the surgical method of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction with double-bundle artificial ligaments based on four-dimensional impingement free mechanism, and to compare its short-term effectiveness with traditional single-bundle reconstruction.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical data of 45 patients with complete ACL rupture who met the selection criteria and were treated between October 2022 and October 2025. Based on anatomical measurement results and surgical technique selection, patients were divided into a single-bundle reconstruction group (29 cases, receiving traditional over-the-top isometric single-bundle reconstruction) and a double-bundle reconstruction group [16 cases, receiving four-dimensional impingement free ACL double-bundle reconstruction (over-the-top anteromedial bundle+low posterolateral bundle)]. Baseline data-including age, injured side, cause of injury, concomitant meniscus injury, and preoperative Lysholm score, International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) score, and Tegner score-showed no significant difference between the two groups ( P>0.05); however, the difference in gender distribution between the two groups was significant ( P<0.05). Operation time, complications, knee range of motion, and the results of the Lachman test, anterior drawer test, and pivot-shift test were recorded. Knee function was evaluated using the Lysholm, IKDC, and Tegner scores preoperatively and at last follow-up, and the proportion of patients returning to pre-injury sports activity levels was calculated. Postoperative three-dimensional CT was performed to evaluate bone tunnel placement and graft-to-tunnel congruence.
RESULTS: Operations were successfully completed in both groups, with the operation time in the double-bundle reconstruction group being significantly longer than that in the single-bundle reconstruction group ( P<0.05). All patients were followed up 6-13 months, with an average of 8.5 months. Patients in both groups resumed immediate postoperative knee range of motion reached 0°-135°, and normal independent walking at 2 weeks postoperatively. At last follow-up, the Lachman test and anterior drawer test were negative in all patients; the pivot-shift test was negative in all cases in the double-bundle reconstruction group, whereas 3 cases (all grade Ⅰ) were positive in the single-bundle reconstruction group, with no significant difference in the positive rate of the pivot-shift test between the two groups ( P>0.05). At last follow-up, the proportion of patients returning to pre-injury sports activity levels was significantly higher in the double-bundle reconstruction group than in the single-bundle reconstruction group ( P<0.05). Both the IKDC and Tegner scores showed significant improvement compared with preoperative values in the two groups ( P<0.05), while the Lysholm scores showed no significant difference when compared with preoperative values ( P>0.05). There was no significant difference in the pre- to post-operative change values of each score between the two groups ( P>0.05). Postoperative three-dimensional CT demonstrated that the distance between the margins of the anterior and posterior bone tunnels in the double-bundle reconstruction group was more than 5 mm, with no evidence of tunnel fracture or posterior cruciate ligament impingement; MRI showed favorable graft morphology without signs of impingement. During the follow-up, no severe complications such as graft laxity, rupture, or synovitis occurred in either group.
CONCLUSION: Under the guarantee of strict anatomical screening, artificial ligament double-bundle reconstruction based on four-dimensional impingement free mechanism shows a favorable clinical trend in restoring rotational stability, with pivot-shift control superior to that of single-bundle reconstruction. Combined with a higher rate of return to sports, it holds significant clinical value for athletic populations seeking early, high-quality rehabilitation. However, strict indication screening based on individualized anatomical conditions is essential for this surgical procedure.

title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects.
METHODS: This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented.
RESULTS: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program.
CONCLUSION: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

title: Posterolateral corner deficiency amplifies varus-related anterior cruciate ligament forces under dynamic loading: A biomechanical study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study examined the influence of varus alignment, posterolateral corner (PLC) insufficiency, and PLC reconstruction on forces acting on the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). It was hypothesized that increasing varus would increase ACL force, PLC transection would amplify this increase, and reconstruction would restore force toward PLC-intact values.
METHODS: Eight cadaveric knees (mean age 62 ± 12 years) underwent dynamic testing at 0°, 10°, 20°, 30° and 40° flexion under 200 N axial load in a materials testing machine with a custom five-degree-of-freedom setup. The ACL was tibially detached and refixated with 80 N using a custom tensioner. Lateral opening-wedge distal femoral osteotomy with external fixation and three-dimensionally printed wedges established 0°, 3°, 5° and 8° varus. Three conditions were tested: (1) native, (2) PLC transection (lateral collateral ligament and popliteus tendon) and (3) PLC reconstruction in Arciero technique.
RESULTS: Axial loading caused ACL forces in PLC-intact knees ranging from 77.1 ± 7.3 N (neutral alignment in 20° flexion) to 109.9 ± 46.8 N (8° varus at 40° flexion). Significant increases in ACL forces were observed at 30° (p = 0.006) and 40° (p = 0.001) of flexion with 8° varus. Following PLC transection, significant increases in ACL forces occurred at 5° varus and higher from 10° of flexion onwards, with a notable increase from 80.0 ± 12.3 (neutral) to 153.2 ± 58.4 N (8° varus, 40° flexion, p < 0.001). After PLC reconstruction, no significant effects of varus alignment or flexion on ACL forces were observed (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Under axial compression and simulated varus-thrust loading conditions, varus alignment of 5° or less did not significantly increase ACL forces in PLC-intact knees, whereas 8° varus resulted in significantly increased ACL loading at selected flexion angles. PLC deficiency was associated with greater increases in ACL force with increasing varus alignment.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: NA.

title: Effects of adding sustained natural apophyseal glides on neuropathic pain-related symptoms and clinical outcomes in patients with lateral elbow tendinopathy: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cervical spine dysfunction and neural mechano-sensitivity may contribute to persistent symptoms in lateral elbow tendinopathy (LET), suggesting a potential role for cervical intervention such as sustained natural apophyseal glides (SNAGS) as an adjunct to rehabilitation.
PURPOSE: To investigate whether adding cervical SNAGS to a conventional rehabilitation program (CRP) improves neuropathic pain-related symptoms and signs, pain intensity, handgrip strength, pinch strength, and disability in individuals with LET.
METHODS: Arandomized controlled trial was conducted on52 participantswith unilateral LET, randomlyassigned toa study grouporcontrol group. The control group received aCRP, whereas the study group received the same program plus cervical SNAGS.Both groups were treated twice weekly for 4 weeks. Outcomes includedLeeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs(LANSS), handgrip strength (HGS),lateral pinch strength, fingertip pinch strength, Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS) at rest and during activity, and Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE). Outcomes were assessed before and after treatment.
RESULTS: Both groups demonstrated significant pre-to-post improvements across all outcomes (p < .001). Between-group analysis of change scores favored the study group for LANSS (p = .049, r_rb = 0.314), HGS (p < .001, r_rb = 1.000), lateral pinch strength (p < .001, r_rb = 1.000), and PRTEE (p = .001, r_rb = 0.521). No significant between-group differences were found for fingertip pinch strength (p = .343, r_rb = 0.152), NPRS at rest (p = .089, r_rb = 0.277), or NPRS during activity (p = .067, r_rb = 0.283). Baseline-adjusted analysis favored the study group for LANSS (p = .008), HGS (p < .001), lateral pinch strength (p < .001), fingertip pinch strength (p = .001), NPRS during activity (p = .034), and PRTEE (p = .001), whereas NPRS at rest did not differ significantly between groups (p = .105).
CONCLUSION: Adding cervical SNAGS to a CRP resulted in greater short-term improvement in several clinically relevant outcomes in individuals with LET.These findings support cervical SNAGS as a useful adjunct within a multimodal rehabilitation approach for LET.Clinical Trial Registry number: Prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06271915).

title: Characterizing accuracy, retention, and dose-response of an 18-session real-time gait biofeedback program following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Individuals following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) commonly demonstrate aberrant walking biomechanics, characterized by a lesser first peak vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) during early stance. Gait biofeedback may address this deficit; however, the accuracy, retention, and dose-response characteristics of repeated training remain unclear.
METHODS: Thirteen individuals (8 females and 5 males; age 22.4 ± 3.4 years; 32.6 ± 18.7 months post-ACLR) completed 18 gait biofeedback sessions over 6 weeks. Participants completed rehabilitation and exhibited involved limb first peak vGRF ≤1.12 body weight (BW) during baseline assessment of treadmill walking. Bilateral, step-by-step visual biofeedback targeted a first peak vGRF of 1.15 BW. Feedback was continuous during sessions 1-10 and was partially tapered thereafter. Outcomes included first peak vGRF target accuracy, defined as the percentage of steps within ±1% of the 1.15 BW target, first peak vGRF during retention, and the estimated training dose required to achieve target loading.
FINDINGS: First peak vGRF target accuracy increased in both limbs from ∼13% during session 1 and plateaued by session 12 (20-25%). Retention testing of the involved limb showed significantly higher first peak vGRF than baseline beginning at session 3, with these improvements maintained through session 18. The median effective dose to achieve target loading was 5 sessions (95% confidence interval: 3-14 sessions).
INTERPRETATION: Bilateral first peak vGRF target accuracy improved across training, while involved-limb improvements were retained before completing the 18-session protocol. These findings support the feasibility of shorter gait biofeedback regimens and provide clinically relevant dosing parameters to inform future clinical trials.

title: Role of the posterior tibial tendon in plantar pressure distribution across progressive stages of ligamentous insufficiency in a cadaveric flatfoot model.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Progressive collapsing foot deformity involves failure of both static and dynamic medial arch stabilizers. The relative timing and interaction between posterior tibial tendon dysfunction and ligamentous attenuation remain unclear. This study investigates whether the posterior tibial tendon can compensate for progressive ligament failure in distributing pressure under the foot in a cadaveric progressive collapsing foot deformity model at balanced stance.
METHODS: Eight cadaveric lower limbs underwent sequential ligament transections replicating progressive collapsing foot deformity. Plantar pressure was recorded during balanced stance using TekScan sensors under both loaded and unloaded posterior tibial tendon conditions. Axial and tendon loads mimicked physiologic forces. Medial-lateral and hindfoot-forefoot pressure ratios were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
FINDINGS: Unloading the posterior tibial tendon significantly increased hindfoot-to-forefoot loading ratios and shifted the center of pressure posteriorly across all ligamentous transection stages (P < 0.05). Medial-to-lateral loading for the entire foot shifted laterally only after the deltoid ligament transection (P = 0.016). In intact feet and short and long plantar ligament conditions, posterior tibial tendon unloading caused a medial shift in hindfoot force (P = 0.039 and P = 0.016, respectively).
INTERPRETATION: This study demonstrates the posterior tibial tendon plays a critical role in distributing plantar load and minimizing hindfoot overload through various stages of ligamentous failure. While posterior tibial tendon unloading consistently increased hindfoot loading, its influence on medial-lateral balance was variable. These findings support early interventions that preserve or augment posterior tibial tendon function to maintain biomechanical stability of the hindfoot.

title: Early sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing characteristics and six-month knee extensor strength after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether quadriceps motor unit firing rates measured pre-operatively and during the first three months after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction are associated with isometric knee extensor strength at six months, and to explore the relationship between motor unit action potential (MUAP) amplitude and firing rate.
METHODS: Twenty-seven participants (15 female) underwent surface electromyography of vastus medialis and vastus lateralis during sub-maximal isometric knee extension from pre-operation to three months post-reconstruction. Six-month knee extensor MVC force was modelled using Bayesian regression and interpreted using a region of practical equivalence (ROPE; ±15 N). A secondary hierarchical analysis examined MUAP amplitude and firing rate.
RESULTS: Motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with six-month knee extensor strength across time points and limbs. In the ACL reconstructed limb at two weeks, a 1-SD greater mean firing rate was associated with 45.8 N greater six-month strength (95% credible interval [CrI] - 18.5 to 114.6 N). Six-month strength was greater in the contralateral limb (β = 198.4 N, 95% CrI 171.6 to 225.1 N), in males (β = 184.3 N, 95% CrI 32.0 to 325.1 N), and with greater body mass (β = 119.9 N per 1-SD, 95% CrI 33.4 to 207.2 N). Greater relative MUAP amplitude was associated with lower firing rate (-3.7 Hz per 1-SD, 95% CrI -3.8 to -3.6 Hz).
CONCLUSIONS: Sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with later knee extensor strength, although a stronger positive association was suggested in the reconstructed limb at two weeks. Firing rate was strongly related to relative MUAP amplitude, and its predictive value for later strength appears limited.

title: Shear wave elastography for assessing lower extremity muscle stiffness after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) restores passive joint stability, yet athletes who meet strength benchmarks may still land stiffly, hesitate to push off, and re-injure. Muscle stiffness governs how rapidly force is transmitted to the joint, and shear wave elastography (SWE) quantifies it muscle by muscle, but SWE findings after ACLR have not been synthesized.
METHODS: Scopus, PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and CINAHL were searched through November 2025 following PRISMA 2020. Eligible studies compared SWE-derived lower-extremity muscle stiffness after ACLR with contralateral limbs or controls. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and appraised quality (Downs and Black). Findings were synthesized narratively with Hedges' g (95% confidence intervals) where data permitted.
FINDINGS: Six studies (173 ACLR participants, 79 controls; quality poor to good) were included. Reduced passive vastus medialis shear modulus was consistently observed in operative limbs (g - 1.10 to -1.21 versus controls) and was associated with quadriceps strength, knee function, and landing biomechanics. Semitendinosus stiffness was reduced after hamstring tendon harvest (g - 1.29 to -1.64) but not at mid-belly after return to sport. Longitudinal deficits persisted at three months; active-contraction findings conflicted. No study sampled the distal vastus medialis obliquus or the distal hamstring musculotendinous region.
INTERPRETATION: SWE detects muscle-specific mechanical deficits that relate to function beyond strength: a compliant vastus medialis offers a mechanical explanation for the strong patient who lands stiffly, and reduced semitendinosus stiffness marks donor-site morbidity. Standardized protocols that sample clinically relevant regions and follow patients to return to sport are needed before SWE can guide rehabilitation.

title: Corrigendum: Scaffold-free bioprinted osteogenic and chondrogenic systems to model osteochondral physiology (2019 Biomed. Mater. 14 065010.
abstract: Three-dimensional bioprinted culture platforms mimic the native microenvironment of tissues more accurately than two-dimensional cell cultures or animal models. Scaffold-free bioprinting eliminates many complications associated with traditional scaffold-dependent printing as well as provides better cell-to-cell interactions and long-term functionality. In this study, constructs were produced from bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) using a scaffold-free bioprinter. These constructs were cultured in either osteogenic, chondrogenic, a 50:50 mixture of osteogenic and chondrogenic ('osteo-chondro), or BM-MSC growth medium. Osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation capacity was determined over an 8-week culture period using histological and immunohistochemical staining and RT-qPCR (Phase I). After 6 weeks in culture, individual osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiated constructs were adhered to create a bone-cartilage interaction model. Adhered differentiated constructs were cultured for an additional 8 weeks in either chondrogenic or osteo-chondro medium to evaluate sustainability of lineage specification and transdifferentiation potential (Phase II).Constructs cultured in their respective osteogenic and/or chondrogenic medium differentiated directly into bone (model of intramembranous ossification) or cartilage. Positive histological and immunohistochemical staining for bone or cartilage identification was shown after 4 and 8 weeks in culture. Expression of osteogenesis and chondrogenesis associated genes increased between weeks 2 and 6. Adhered individual osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiated constructs sustained their differentiated phenotype when cultured in chondrogenic medium. However, adhered individual chondrogenic differentiated constructs cultured in osteo-chondro medium were converted to bone (model of metaplastic transformation).These bioprinted models of bone-cartilage interaction, intramembranous ossification, and metaplastic transformation of cartilage into bone offer a useful and promising approach for bone and cartilage tissue engineering research. Specifically, these models can be potentially used as functional tissue systems for studying osteochondral defect repair, drug discovery and response, and many other potential applications.&#xD.

title: Efficacy of Autologous Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injections in the Management of Presbyphonia.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical, auditory-perceptual, aerodynamic, and acoustic outcomes of serial autologous Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) injections administered via an in-office approach in a cohort of patients with presbyphonia.
METHODS: A single-center retrospective analysis was conducted on 36 patients (mean age 72.78 years) diagnosed with presbyphonia who underwent two to three serial PRP injections into the thyroarytenoid muscle between October 2021 and April 2025. Pre and post treatment evaluations included patient self-assessment via a 0-10 Visual Analog Scale for vocal handicap, auditory-perceptual analysis using the GRB scale, Maximum Phonation Time (MPT), acoustic parameters (F0, Jitter, HNR), and stroboscopic mucosal wave grading.
RESULTS: Thirty-five patients completed the primary protocol. Patient self-assessment scores demonstrated a highly significant reduction in perceived vocal handicap post-intervention (from 7.17 to 4.57, P < 0.0001, r = 0.584). Auditory-perceptual analysis revealed significant improvements across all GRB scale components, notably the overall Grade (P = 0.0002) and Roughness (P < 0.0001). MPT significantly increased from 11.47 to 13.31 seconds (P = 0.018). Conversely, traditional objective acoustic parameters showed no statistically significant post-treatment changes. Stroboscopic evaluation demonstrated improved mucosal wave dynamics in 82.9% of patients, which strongly correlated with self-assessment gains (ρ = 0.496, P = 0.0024). Baseline severity was a significant predictor of treatment response.
CONCLUSIONS: Serial office-based autologous PRP injections offer a safe, well-tolerated, and effective biological treatment for presbyphonia. By improving mucosal pliability and reducing perceived vocal handicap, PRP bridges the gap between conservative therapy and invasive surgical interventions, serving as a valuable regenerative tool for the aging voice.

title: Nano-kinetic implant surface mediates osteo-antibacterial synergy through electromagnetic-mechanical coupling.
abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a devastating complication of total joint arthroplasty, mainly caused by bacterial biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance. Traditional static surfaces rely on contact killing-based bactericidal properties and cannot reliably clear mature biofilms. In this study, we fabricate a remote-activated dynamic biomimetic system, namely a movable magnetic topographic surface (MMTS). Here we show that under the exposure of external electromagnetic field (EMF), the anchored Janus nano-heterodimers oscillate periodically to mechanically disrupt bacterial membranes and eradicates biofilms of Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. This mechanical force can also activates Piezo1 mechanosensitive ion channel in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), inducing calcium oscillations, upregulating gene expression of Runx2 and BMP2, and enhancing extracellular matrix mineralization. In vivo, MMTS combined with EMF exposure eliminates local infection and promoted osseointegration. This remote-activated dynamic biomimetic strategy offers a promising multifunctional platform for PJI treatment, and improved implant osteointegration in clinical orthopedics.

title: Intensity-dependent microcurrent stimulation enhances BMSC-derived cartilage microtissue formation under defined culture conditions.
abstract: Engineering phenotypically favorable cartilage-like tissue from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) remains challenging because chondrogenic differentiation can be accompanied by insufficient cartilage-associated extracellular matrix accumulation and unfavorable hypertrophic and catabolic responses. Here, we established a microcurrent-assisted culture system for scaffold-free BMSC-derived cartilage microtissues (CMTs) and investigated the intensity-dependent effects of continuous unidirectional direct-current stimulation at 0, 50, 100, 150, 250, or 500 μA under a defined electrical and culture configuration. Among the tested conditions, 150 μA (nominal electrode current density, 3 μA/mm2) showed the most consistently favorable overall response, with enhanced cartilage-associated gene and protein expression, greater type II collagen- and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix accumulation, improved CMT morphology, and higher apparent mechanical properties. In contrast, 250 and 500 μA were associated with reduced cartilage-associated matrix formation and increased fibrotic, hypertrophic, catabolic, inflammatory, and apoptosis-related markers. The 150 μA condition was also associated with a distinct intracellular Ca2+ response pattern and increased NFATc1 nuclear localization; verapamil, BAPTA-AM, and cyclosporin A attenuated NFATc1 nuclear localization, supporting involvement of Ca2+/calcineurin/NFAT-related signaling without establishing a unique causal mechanism. After 2 weeks of xenogeneic subcutaneous implantation in nude mice, CMTs preconditioned at 150 μA exhibited greater cartilage-like matrix accumulation and higher apparent compressive properties than those preconditioned at 0 or 500 μA. These findings identify 150 μA as the best-performing tested condition under the present electrical configuration and provide short-term ectopic proof-of-concept evidence, while longer-term orthotopic studies are required to evaluate phenotypic stability, tissue integration, and functional outcomes in cartilage-defect models.

title: A distributed event-triggered framework for coordinating athlete autonomic states via wearable sensor networks.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Interpersonal autonomic physiology (IAP) research has established that physiological synchrony (PS), the temporal interdependence of autonomic nervous system (ANS) activity across individuals, is an established phenomenon in team-based settings. However, PS in athlete cohorts has been studied exclusively as a passive observational variable; no framework actively regulates autonomic coherence under the communication constraints of wireless body area networks. This study integrates IAP and distributed control theory by formulating team-level autonomic coherence as a leaderless multi-agent consensus problem.
METHODS: Each wearable unit was modeled as a two-dimensional linear agent whose state encodes cardiovascular autonomic tone (parasympathetic index: HRV-RMSSD) and sympathetic arousal load (EDA skin-conductance level, SCL), consistent with the Banister Fitness-Fatigue Model. Initial model states were derived from ECG/EDA records of WESAD subjects S2-S7, used only to provide heterogeneous simulation initial conditions (correlations were directional, non-significant sanity checks: r = -0.71, p = 0.114 for RMSSD; r = 0.68, p = 0.137 for SCL; N = 6). Three engineering challenges were addressed: (i) BLE communication delays h c ∈ [15, 150] ms; (ii) neuromuscular input delays h i ∈ [150, 300] ms; and (iii) switching directed topologies from dynamic team formations. A distributed dynamic event-triggered mechanism (DETM) drove all agents toward consensus while transmitting data only upon detection of meaningful state deviation. Stability was established via a dual-integral Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional, with LMI feasibility verified by CVXPY (ε = 0.087). Simulations ran for 300 s under three delay scenarios with five initial-condition perturbation folds; battery life was estimated from a four-component nRF52840 energy model.
RESULTS: The proposed DETM reduced BLE transmissions by 38.38% in the nominal case while achieving convergence of the normalized model states within 4-7 s. A Zeno-free guarantee (T min = 0.06 s) and a theoretical battery-life estimate of about 36 days were obtained. The ablation analysis attributed the largest communication saving to the dynamic internal variable ρ i (t) and the largest convergence-time improvement to the dual-delay structure. Five initial-condition perturbation folds indicated numerical robustness to the starting states.
DISCUSSION: These findings support control-theoretic and network-level feasibility only. Athlete studies are required before physiological benefits, safety, or real-world effectiveness can be inferred.

title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation and Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation in Athletes: Optimizing Athletic Performance and Sleep Quality Through Neuromodulation.
abstract: Neuromodulation is a procedure relying on the delivery of specific stimuli to selected sites of the nervous system and hereby influencing its activity. Even though the underlying neurobiological mechanisms are not yet fully elucidated and the research is still ongoing, neuromodulation is already being used as an intervention for various mental conditions and insomnia, or it may even improve the physical performance of athletes. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the effects of specific neuromodulation techniques on performance and sleep quality in athletes, focusing on cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). PubMed, SCOPUS, Web of Science and Ovid MEDLINE databases were searched for relevant articles. All types of publications were taken into account, but original studies, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and meta-analyses were given priority. Current evidence shows that while tDCS may improve athletic performance, especially endurance and sport-specific skills, its impact on sleep in athletes is inconclusive. This method may increase subjectively reported total sleep time and subjective sleep quality, but no objective improvement has been demonstrated. CES findings are preliminary: evidence from the small trials suggests improvement of selected objective sleep parameters, but the evidence base is limited to two small studies, one of which lacked a sham condition. In conclusion, non-invasive neuromodulation methods, specifically tDCS and CES, may impact athletic performance and help treat sleep disorders in athletes. Neuromodulation should not be viewed as a standalone method, but rather a complementary tool to other known interventions for insomnia in athletes. Although the aforementioned techniques show promising results, the research on this topic is limited and requires further evaluation.

title: The Mum-Alete: An Observational Survey-Based Study of Australian Athletes Returning to High-Performance Sport After Pregnancy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: As more female athletes extend their careers and resume high-performance sport following childbirth, there is an increasing need to understand factors influencing this transition. The return-to-high-performance sport process for postpartum athletes remains complex, with limited evidence available to guide sporting organisations and practitioners. This study aimed to identify the experiences, facilitators, challenges, and barriers for athletes returning to high-performance sport postpartum.
DESIGN: An exploratory cross-sectional survey study.
METHODS: Participants included postpartum elite and sub-elite Australian athletes who maintained training 6 months prior to conception and gave birth between July 2016 and February 2022. The online Mum-Alete survey included various types of closed-ended questions as well as open-ended questions to gather deeper insights related to demographic/pregnancy information, training and performance, physical health (e.g., sport-related injuries), and social factors impacting return to high-performance sport. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise data, while a hybrid thematic analysis was used for qualitative analyses.
RESULTS: Descriptive analyses for the 64 athletes who participated showed most resumed exercise within 6-week postpartum, with pelvic floor exercises initiated earliest. Endurance and strength training followed, though 59% of respondents reported performance declines and 43% reported sport-related injuries. Key challenges in returning to high-performance sport included time management, sleep, breastfeeding, and pelvic floor dysfunction. Among facilitators in returning to high-performance sport, support from family, coaches, and medical staff was generally rated positively, with many athletes reporting a lack of (or non-awareness of) organisational policies and support provisions (e.g., well-being officer, maternity leave, status protections, including stipends, caregiver allowance to attend training) as well as facility-related challenges (e.g., dedicated spaces for childcare and breastfeeding). Eight qualitative themes were identified, including time/time management, training 'new' bodies, safe return to high-performance sport, breastfeeding while participating, critical support, navigating motherhood and sport, discrimination, and education/expertise.
CONCLUSIONS: This study showed that while athletes returned to high-performance training relatively early following childbirth, they regularly perceived reductions in performance and reported sport-related injuries. Various factors were also shown to facilitate and challenge the return-to-high-performance sport process. These outcomes highlight the need for athlete-informed, multidisciplinary, and flexible support strategies, and underscore critical gaps in organisational practice.

title: Extreme energy expenditure during a 200 km three-day open-water swim: A doubly labeled water case study.
abstract: The upper limits of total energy expenditure (TEE) in humans have primarily been described during single-day ultra-endurance events, or during multistage land-based endurance events across several days. However, little is known about the physiological limits of sustained energy turnover during shorter multi-day, near-continuous exercise events, particularly when performed in an aquatic environment. Prolonged immersion in water imposes substantial thermoregulatory demands due to increased conductive heat loss, which may further elevate metabolic requirements beyond those observed in (cold) land-based events. The 200 km Elfstedentocht swim, completed over approximately three days with minimal sleep and near-continuous swimming, provides a unique opportunity to investigate the upper limits of human energy expenditure during prolonged multi-day exercise in water. In this case study, we therefore assessed TEE in a former Olympic athlete (mass 103 kg, height 2.04 m, age 38 years) during a 200-km swim completed over 3 days using doubly labeled water. TEE was 195 Megajoule (MJ) (46,700 kcals), corresponding to 6.17x basal metabolic rate over the three-day period. This TEE is among the highest TEE reported thus far over similar periods, suggesting that the combined near-continuous exercise and imposed sustained thermoregulatory demands due to conductive heat loss lead to extreme energy expenditure. Notably, the absolute energy expenditure of ∼14,700 kcal per day exceeds previous limits.
journal: Journal of exercise science and fitness

title: Propionibacterium cheese and bone turnover in active young adults: a randomized-controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Young physically active individuals exposed to prolonged physiological stress and low energy availability are prone to reduced gonadal steroid protection and increased bone turnover. Nutritional strategies that favor positive bone remodeling balance are of clinical interest. Jarlsberg cheese contains Propionibacterium freudenreichii (PF), which produces vitamin K₂ and 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoic acid (DHNA), compounds with potential favorable effects on bone health.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this 24-week sex-stratified randomized-controlled trial, 60 young physically active adults engaged in endurance training were allocated to daily intake of either Jarlsberg cheese or a nutritionally comparable control cheese without PF. The primary outcome was change in serum total osteocalcin (tOC). Secondary outcomes were changes in carboxylated osteocalcin (cOC), procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP), cross-linked C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX), P1NP/CTX ratio, lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD), and trabecular bone score (TBS).
RESULTS: After 24 weeks, serum tOC was significantly higher in the Jarlsberg group than in controls (38.0 vs. 26.8 ng/mL, p < 0.01). cOC and P1NP/CTX ratio increased in favor of the Jarlsberg group (p = 0.03). Lumbar spine BMD increased in the Jarlsberg group (mean change 0.012 g/cm2, p = 0.03), with a greater increase than in controls (p = 0.05), and TBS showed a positive trend in the Jarlsberg group.
CONCLUSION: Daily intake of cheese-containing PF was associated with favorable changes in bone turnover markers and increase in lumbar spine BMD. These findings suggest that PF-fermented cheese may support bone metabolism in young individuals exposed to reduced hormonal protection and high bone turnover.

title: Association Between Hormone Variability and Anaerobic Performance in Recreationally Active Women: An Exploratory Study Using Mixed-Effect Location Scale Models.
abstract: Ramey, KT, Unrein, CL, Yang, C-H, and Hirsch, KR. Association between hormone variability and anaerobic performance in recreationally active women: An exploratory study using mixed-effect location scale models. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study explored the application of mixed-effects location scale modeling (MELS) to examine how daily variability in urinary estrogen (E), progesterone (PdG), and their ratio (E:P) relates to repeated sprint performance (peak power [PP], average power [AP], power drop [PD], and fatigue index [FI]) across low and high hormone phases in healthy, recreationally active eumenorrheic (n = 8) women and hormonal contraceptive users (intrauterine device = 6; oral contraception = 10; age: 24.7 ± 4.2 years; height: 165.5 ± 6.5 cm; body mass: 63.0 ± 6.7 kg). Subjects completed 30.4 ± 10.7 days of at-home urine hormone testing for E (ng⋅ml-1), PdG (µg⋅ml-1), and calculate E:P ratio. A repeated sprint test (10 × [6 seconds sprint: 30 seconds rest]) on a cycle ergometer was completed during both the low and high hormone phases to evaluate sprint performance. Fatigue index (%) was recorded, and PP (W), AP (W), and PD (W) were averaged across sprints. Associations between E, P, and E:P with FI, PP, AP, and PD were examined using separate MELS models. Paired t-tests assessed phase differences, and Pearson correlations evaluated relationships between day-of-testing hormone levels and performance. Day-of-testing E (p < 0.001), PdG (p < 0.001), PP (p = 0.047), and AP (p = 0.016) were significantly higher in the high hormone phase, and PdG correlated positively with PD (r = 0.574, p = 0.003). Greater individual E variability was associated with lower PP (Low: Estimate = -48.47, p = 0.004; High: Estimate = -50.18, p = 0.009) and AP (Low: Estimate = -46.75, p = 0.005; High: Estimate = -42.04, p = 0.024), remaining significant after controlling for percent body fat and lean mass (p = 0.008-0.022). These findings suggest hormonal instability may meaningfully influence anaerobic performance. This study introduces novel methodology and statistical framework that captures dynamic hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle and can be used to evaluate hormonal influence on female physiology and performance variability.
