title: Bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses to short-term low energy availability with and without preserved protein intake: a randomized, controlled, multi-period, cross-over trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Bone appears sensitive to low energy availability (LEA), with prolonged exposure linked to compromised bone health. Causality, however, along with underlying mechanisms, and the role of macronutrient availability remain unclear.
PURPOSE: To investigate the influence of short-term energy and protein manipulation on bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses to acute exercise.
METHODS: Nineteen healthy, active young adults (9 females, 10 males) completed three 5-day dietary conditions in a randomized crossover design: adequate energy availability (AEA; 45 kcal·kgFFM·day-1), LEA (15 kcal·kgFFM·day-1) and LEA with protein matched to AEA (LEA-P). On days 1 and 5, participants completed a standardized exercise protocol comprising 45 min of cycling at 65% of pre-defined peak power output followed by a Wingate test, with blood samples collected at prespecified time-points to assess fasted and post-exercise bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses.
RESULTS: Fasted P1NP was lower following both energy-restricted trials compared with AEA, and remained lower during post-exercise recovery following LEA-P. CTX-1 was higher in the post-exercise recovery period following LEA-P only. Multiple inflammatory cytokines (IL6, IL8, IL10, ILRa, and IL1β) increased at distinct time-points in both energy-restricted trials. Overall, evidence for condition effects relative to AEA was more consistent following LEA-P than LEA.
CONCLUSION: Short-term energy restriction suppressed biomarkers indicative of bone formation and augmented the inflammatory cytokine response to exercise, with some, but less consistent evidence for increased bone resorption. Preserving protein intake did not attenuate these effects. In contrast, this condition was associated with more consistent and pronounced perturbations, potentially reflecting reduced carbohydrate availability rather than protein per se.

title: Effect of Adjunctive Mifepristone Pre-treatment on Operative Efficiency and Postoperative Recovery in Cesarean Scar Pregnancy Undergoing Curettage After Uterine Artery Embolization.
abstract:
AIM: This study aims to evaluate whether short-course mifepristone pre-treatment improves procedural efficiency and early recovery after uterine artery embolization (UAE), followed by dilation and curettage (D&C) for cesarean scar pregnancy.
METHODS: This retrospective study recruited 108 patients with cesarean scar pregnancy who underwent dilation and D&C between January 2020 and July 2023. Patients were divided into 2 groups according to the pre-treatment approach. The control group (n = 65) received pre-treatment with UAE alone, while the study group (n = 43) received pre-treatment with mifepristone in addition to the treatment used in the control group. The two groups were compared for operative metrics, early recovery, and postoperative adverse events. Serum β-human chorionic gonadotrophin (β-hCG) levels were evaluated upon admission and again on postoperative day 1. Patients were followed for one year to assess pregnancy-related outcomes, and the findings were compared between the two groups.
RESULTS: In the study group, the surgery duration was shorter, and the intraoperative blood loss was lower than in the control group (p < 0.05). The length of hospital stay was comparable between the two groups (p > 0.05). Similarly, the incidences of repeat D&C, massive hemorrhage, and re-embolization of the uterine artery were also comparable between groups (p > 0.05). There were no cases of conversion to laparotomy or hysterectomy in either group. At the time of admission, the β-hCG levels in the study group were not significantly different from those in the control group. However, on the first day after the procedure, the β-hCG levels in the study group were lower than those in the control group, but the difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.051). The study group had a shorter duration of vaginal bleeding and achieved normal menstrual function earlier than the control group (p < 0.05). The menstrual cycle was comparable between the two groups (p > 0.05). The incidences of fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, abnormal liver function, and intrauterine adhesions were also comparable between the two groups (p > 0.05). Follow-up analysis showed no significant differences between the two groups in subsequent pregnancy or recurrence of cesarean scar pregnancy (p > 0.05). Time to pregnancy was descriptively reported only among patients who achieved pregnancy and was not statistically compared because of the small number of events.
CONCLUSIONS: Incorporating short-course mifepristone pre-treatment to a standard uterine artery embolization-D&C strategy for cesarean scar pregnancy was associated with shorter operative time and better early recovery profiles, with satisfactory safety outcomes.

title: Talking about menstruation in professional women's sport: gendered communication between athletes, coaches and team-mates.
abstract: Communication about menstruation remains uneven within sporting environments despite growing recognition of the importance of menstrual health for athletes. This article investigates how female athletes communicate about menstruation and how gendered hierarchies shape these interactions. The analysis is based on responses to an online questionnaire completed by Polish professional athletes (N = 253). The findings indicate that menstruation is seldom discussed between athletes and coaches, with participants identifying social and institutional barriers, including menstrual taboo and the predominance of male coaches. In contrast, athletes reported discussing menstruation more openly with female team-mates, where such conversations often facilitated mutual support and the sharing of experiential knowledge about menstrual health. These interactions suggest that women's teams can function as 'counterspaces' where menstrual experiences can be acknowledged and normalised in ways largely absent from coach-athlete relationships. Findings highlight the importance of creating environments in which menstrual health can be openly discussed, as limited communication about menstruation may restrict athletes' access to information, support, and health-related guidance. By examining menstruation as a topic of health-related communication, the study contributes to scholarship on gender, embodiment and menstrual health, highlighting how institutional hierarchies shape the visibility and discussion of bodily processes across different social contexts.

title: [Disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders among athletes II.].
abstract: Over the past two and a half decades, a substantial shift has occurred in the understanding of disordered eating and eating disorders among athletes. Research has gradually moved beyond the concept of the female athlete triad towards the model of relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), which recognizes low energy availability as a key factor affecting both athletes' health and performance. The aim of this study is to review the international literature published between 2000 and 2025 on disordered eating and eating disorders in athletes, with particular emphasis on prevalence, the contemporary interpretation of risk factors, the development of the REDs concept, and current recommendations for screening, treatment, and prevention. A thematic narrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Scopus databases. Publications and professional consensus statements addressing disordered eating, eating disorders, relative energy deficiency, screening, prevention, and multidisciplinary care in athletes were included in the analysis. The reviewed literature indicates that disordered eating behaviors are considerably more prevalent than clinically diagnosed eating disorders; however, both conditions adversely affect athletes' health and performance. The evidence also confirms that low energy availability is not exclusively associated with eating disorders but may also result from an imbalance between energy intake and exercise expenditure. The introduction of the REDs model substantially expanded the earlier female athlete triad concept by highlighting the involvement of male athletes, the role of psychological factors, and the multisystem consequences of low energy availability. Current international recommendations emphasize early identification, sport-specific risk assessment, and multidisciplinary care as the cornerstones of effective prevention and treatment. Contemporary approaches to nutrition-related problems in athletes consider disordered eating, eating disorders, and relative energy deficiency as interrelated conditions. The development of standardized multidisciplinary models of care consistent with current international recommendations would be warranted in Hungary. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1702-1709.

title: Young Investigator Award: Where Do We Start? A Conceptual Model for Implementing Menstrual Cycle Tracking in Sport.
abstract: Menstrual cycle tracking is a much-discussed component of the ' female athlete' research theme; however, more translational work is needed to meet practitioners' desire for further guidance on the implementation of tracking in applied settings. The purpose of this paper is to present a preliminary conceptual model to inform practitioners' decision-making around menstrual cycle tracking and assist researchers in identifying and framing future research directions. The proposed model-Conducting and Navigating menstrual cycle Education, Communication and Tracking (ConNECT)-proposes that communication and education strategies may be utilised to affect social, organisational and individual level change, ultimately supporting the implementation of menstrual cycle tracking by increasing its uptake and impact. This model was developed based on the findings from a series of studies conducted by the authors, which considered the existing literature on tracking and the perspectives of athletes and practitioners. Therefore, the ConNECT model offers an ecologically sound starting point for sport scientists, coaches and other members of an athlete's support team to base their practice on.

title: Baseline Symptom Collection in Elite Rugby Union Players-Limited Clinical Utility? An Investigation of Assessments Across 5879 men and Women Athletes.
abstract: In World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment (HIA) protocol, a modified Sports Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) is completed during the pre-season (baseline) and when a player has a suspected head injury. The symptom component of the SCAT, which involves comparing current to baseline symptoms, has been shown to be the most predictive component for concussion diagnosis. Because the clinical comparison of symptom report to baseline is a key determinant of concussion diagnosis, this study aims to explore the relationship between symptoms endorsement at baseline and during HIA. Mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) are presented along with relevant bivariate analyses. Logistic regressions compared proportions of symptom endorsement profiles between men and women. At baseline, 'Trouble sleeping' and 'Fatigue or low energy' were commonly reported symptoms for men and women. At baseline, women (mean + SD) reported more symptoms than men (mean + SD) on average. During the HIA, women players were nearly 3 times (Relative risk: 2.98 95% CIs: 2.47-3.60) more likely than men to report fewer symptoms immediately after the match than at baseline (47% women vs. 16% men). While this study highlights the importance of collecting baseline assessment as a medical overview of players, it de-emphasises the relevance of baseline symptoms when using the SCAT as a clinical assessment tool in professional rugby players. This study also highlights important differences in men and women's rugby players in symptom reporting, and recommends de-coupling baseline symptom reporting from the diagnostic part of the HIA.

title: Female Athletes Are Half as Likely to Return to High-Risk Sports Compared With Male Athletes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: An Exploration of Return-to-Sport Outcomes Between Sexes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Differences in female and male athletes' return-to-sport (RTS) outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) are not well understood. The purpose of this study was to explore sex-based differences in RTS rates and predictors of RTS after ACLR for athletes participating in high-risk sports.
HYPOTHESIS: Female athletes will have significantly lower RTS rates than male athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial comparing single-bundle hamstring tendon autograft ACLR with or without a lateral extra-articular tenodesis using the iliotibial band.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 1.
METHODS: Data from 500 patients who underwent ACLR and participated in high-risk (jumping, pivoting, cutting) sport before injury were included in the study. Three definitions of RTS were created: return to preinjury sport and level, return to any high-risk sport at any level, and return to any sport at any level. Return rates were reported for the overall sample, and separately for male and female athletes. Multivariable logistic regression models were constructed to investigate predictors of each RTS outcome.
RESULTS: Approximately 86.5% of patients returned to any sport, whereas 76.5% returned to a high-risk sport, and only 45.5% returned to their preinjury high-risk sport and level. Male athletes reported consistently higher RTS rates than female athletes. In the final model predicting return to high-risk sport, female athletes had 53% lower odds of returning to high-risk sports compared with male athletes (odds ratio [OR], 0.47; 95% CI, 0.29 to 0.76; P < 0.01). For female athletes, earlier surgical intervention, higher confidence in the knee, and a stable knee were significant predictors of returning to high-risk sport.
CONCLUSION: Female athletes are less likely to RTS after ACLR compared with their male counterparts; however, this discrepancy appears greatest for athletes returning to high-risk sports.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Female athletes in high-risk sports may be an important target population for interventions to improve RTS rates after ACLR, and psychological readiness and knee stability may be important treatment targets within this group.

title: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium in adolescent athletes with acute groin pain: clinical and MRI features of a radiograph-occult injury pattern.
abstract: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is an uncommon MRI finding in young athletes with acute groin pain and is frequently occult on plain radiographs. This study aimed to characterize its clinical presentation, MRI findings, associated injuries, and return-to-sport outcomes. This retrospective single-center case series included athletes aged ≤22 years who underwent MRI for acute sports-related groin pain with negative or inconclusive radiographs between 2017 and 2025. Patients meeting predefined MRI criteria for subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium were identified, and clinical, imaging, and outcome data were analyzed descriptively. Twenty of 91 patients (22.0%) met the MRI criteria. Their mean age was 13.9 ± 1.5 years, 19 (95%) were male, and 18 (90%) had open physes. Periosteal elevation was present in all patients, and 19 (95%) demonstrated a predominantly subperiosteal fluid collection, most commonly with a lentiform configuration. Associated anterior inferior iliac spine avulsion injury or intramuscular iliacus injury was identified in 10 patients (50%). All patients were managed nonoperatively and returned to unrestricted sports participation after progressive rehabilitation at a mean of 4.5 ± 2.2 weeks. Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is a reproducible MRI finding in predominantly skeletally immature athletes with acute sports-related groin pain and negative or inconclusive radiographs. Recognition of periosteal elevation with a predominantly subperiosteal fluid collection may facilitate diagnosis of this radiograph-occult injury pattern. Although the underlying injury mechanism remains hypothetical, prospective studies are needed to clarify its clinical significance.

title: Arthroscopic Circumferential Labral Repair and Biceps Tenodesis in Elite Throwing Athletes: Technical Considerations.
abstract: SLAP lesions are a common cause of shoulder pain in overhead athletes and are often seen together with circumferential labral tearing, partial-thickness rotator cuff tearing, and biceps pathology. Isolated repair of the superior labrum has produced inconsistent outcomes, with low return-to-play rates in professional throwers. In patients with these complex cases, instability and anterior shoulder pain often coexist, and isolated labral repair or tenodesis may not be adequate treatment. Conversely, tenodesis without superior labral repair may increase glenohumeral translation. The senior author believes long head of the biceps tendon release reduces traction on the SLAP repair and may support healing. We describe an arthroscopic technique for circumferential labral repair, with knotless all-suture anchors performed in the beach-chair position, combined with open subpectoral biceps tenodesis and adjunct subacromial decompression. This technique restores stability, removes the biceps as a pain generator, eliminates traction on the repaired labrum, and preserves motion.

title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions.
METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot.
RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance.
CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.

title: Summary of the 2026 Professionals in Nutrition for Exercise and Sport "10 Questions/10 Experts" Session-Are Sports Nutrition Guidelines Too Elite Focused for Recreational Athletes?
abstract: This article provides a synopsis of the 10 Questions/10 Experts session at the 2026 American College of Sports Medicine Annual Meeting, which examined whether sports nutrition guidelines are equally applicable from recreational to elite athletes. Each speaker considered the validity of a given common "myth" statement and provided an evidence-based opinion to support, bust, or qualify propositions addressing the following questions: (a) Are sports nutrition guidelines based primarily on studies of elite athletes, and are they too serious for recreational athletes? (b) Do recreational marathon runners need the same in-race carbohydrate recommendations as elite marathon runners? (c) Must recreational athletes consume 1.6 g·kg-1·day-1 of protein to benefit from exercise training? (d) Does nitrate supplementation benefit elite and recreational athletes equally? (e) Do recreational athletes need a structured fluid intake plan? (f) Is sodium bicarbonate loading relevant only to elite athletes? (g) Do recreational and elite athletes require more micronutrients than suggested by the Recommended Dietary Allowances? (h) Is eating after 8:00 p.m. detrimental to performance or recovery in recreational athletes? (i) Are recreational athletes at greater risk for suboptimal vitamin D status because indoor occupations reduce sunlight exposure? and (j) Should recreational athletes train with low carbohydrate availability to amplify adaptation? This article describes the content of each presentation, including the most important evidence, practical implications, and conclusions identified by the presenters.
journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism

title: Reliability of a functional electromechanical dynamometer for a bilateral standing press exercise at intensities of 30% and 60% of isometric peak force in trained women.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Determining the reliability of exercise instruments and protocols in the fields of health and sports performance is of great interest due to their close relationship with monitoring and decision-making in athletes. Studies in trained women are limited, and more evidence is needed on performance variables and the reliability of exercise protocols.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of an exercise protocol for determining mean muscle strength, mean velocity, and mean power during the bilateral standing press (BSP) in trained women.
METHODS: Sixteen trained women (age = 20.0 ± 2.30 years; body mass = 67.63 ± 6.68 kg; height = 1.65 ± 0.06 m) participated in this repeated-measures study. Absolute reliability was assessed using the coefficient of variation (CV), and relative reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for a bilateral standing press (BSP) exercise protocol performed at intensities of 30% and 60% of isometric peak force (IPF).
RESULTS: Mean muscle strength showed acceptable absolute reliability and extremely high relative reliability at both 30% IPF (CV = 6.51%; ICC = 0.94) and 60% IPF (CV = 5.03%; ICC = 0.97). Mean velocity showed extremely high relative reliability at 60% IPF (ICC = 0.92), but its absolute reliability was not acceptable at either 30% IPF (CV = 10.10%; ICC = 0.75) or 60% IPF (CV = 14.16%; ICC = 0.92). Mean power also exceeded the predefined CV threshold at 30% IPF (CV = 11.16%; ICC = 0.85) and at 60% IPF (CV = 14.35%; ICC = 0.89).
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that the BSP protocol using functional electromechanical dynamometry is reliable for assessing mean muscle strength in trained women. However, mean velocity and mean power should be interpreted with caution, as their absolute reliability did not reach the predefined threshold of acceptable reliability.

title: A multimodal framework to assess differences in dynamic visual acuity between athletes with and without recent sport-related concussion.
abstract: Sport-related concussions (SRC) commonly affect vision and cognition, but there is limited understanding of how concurrent balance and exertion demands may affect visual-cognitive performance beyond symptom resolution.Purpose To determine if a dynamic visual acuity (DVA) task performed during standing and walking could differentiate performance between athletes with and without concussion history.Methods Interuniversity athletes (N = 30, age = 20.9 years ± 1.4) with SRC history who were asymptomatic (SRC = 14; females = 6) were compared to athletes without SRC (CONTROL = 16; female = 7). A DVA task was completed while seated, standing, and during low- and moderate-intensity treadmill walking. A Tumbling 'E' target was presented randomly in either random walk (R) or horizontal (H) motion (2.31 m/s), in one of four orientations; responses were selected using a handheld keypad. Performance was characterized as a change in DVA score from Seated (logMAR) and response time (RT, ms). A linear mixed-effects model was fitted for DVA change scores and a generalized mixed effects model for median RT.Results The SRC group exhibited worse DVA change scores during standing and walking compared to CONTROL (p < .05) during R-motion only. Whereas both groups responded faster during treadmill walking for both R- and H-motion (p < .001). Only two athletes (14%) in the SRC group experienced mild symptoms that did not affect performance during the protocol.Conclusion A multimodal DVA assessment, including standing and walking conditions, may be a feasible approach to detect differences in visual-cognitive performance for athletes following clinical recovery of concussion.

title: The Hidden Cost: Effects of Prior Coordinative, Sprint, and Combined Tasks on Physical Performance During Small-Sided Games in Youth Soccer Players.
abstract: This study compared the effects of sprint (SPRT), coordinative (COORD), and combined (COMB) exercises on physical performance in small-sided games (SSGs). Twenty-four under-16 male soccer players participated in a repeated-measures design, performing four interventions (Control [CONT], SPRT, COORD, and COMB) prior to SSGs in a 4v4+GK format. The total distance, distance covered in different speed zones, acceleration, and deceleration were analyzed. Data were assessed using generalized estimating equations, adopting p ≤ .05 for statistical significance. A lower total distance (p = .02) and shorter distances in the initial acceleration zones (0.0-0.99 m·s-2; p = .013) were observed after COMB compared with CONT. A similar result was also observed in the deceleration zone between -2.00 and -2.99 m·s-2, where a lower value was found after COMB compared to CONT (p = .043). Furthermore, COMB (p = .021) and SPRT (p = .023) reduced the number of decelerations compared with CONT. Overall, the combined condition was associated with selective reductions in specific physical performance variables during subsequent SSGs, whereas most speed-zone, acceleration, and deceleration variables remained unchanged. Therefore, combined coordinative and sprint tasks should be incorporated with caution when SSGs are intended to provide a high physical stimulus.
journal: Research quarterly for exercise and sport

title: Effects of Integrative Neuromuscular Training on Unilateral and Bilateral Lower-Extremity Sports Performance in Adolescent Female Sprinters: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent female athletes often exhibit more pronounced lower-limb asymmetry due to physiological differences, increasing injury risk. Despite documented efficacy in team sports for injury mitigation and performance enhancement, integrative neuromuscular training (INT) effects on unilateral and bilateral lower-limb capabilities in trained adolescent female sprinters remain undetermined.
HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that an 8-week INT program would significantly improve unilateral and bilateral lower-extremity performance measures in adolescent female sprinters compared with traditional sprint-specific training.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 1.
METHODS: Twenty-four national second-level adolescent female sprinters (aged 16-18 years) were randomly assigned to an 8-week INT group (n = 12) or a control group (CON, n = 12) that continued traditional sprint-specific training. Measurements obtained before and after the intervention included the hop test, star excursion balance test (SEBT), 3-repetition maximum (3RM) unilateral and bilateral back squat, 100-m run, standing long jump (SLJ), and limb symmetry index (LSI).
RESULTS: After the intervention, the INT group outperformed the CON group on the nondominant side in all hop tests (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.74-0.88), six directions of the SEBT (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.44-0.88), and the 3RM unilateral back squat (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.65). On the dominant side, the INT group also outperformed the CON group in the single hop for distance (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.80) and three directions of the SEBT (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.38-0.84). In addition, the INT group showed significantly greater improvements than the CON group in the LSI from unilateral tests (all P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.26-0.88), as well as in the 100-m run and SLJ (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.61-0.69).
CONCLUSION: The 8-week INT program was associated with improvements in dynamic balance, explosive power, and limb symmetry in adolescent female sprinters, with greater benefits observed on the nondominant side.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: INT is an effective training modality for improving lower-limb performance and mitigating asymmetry in adolescent female sprinters.

title: Clinical and functional predictors of delayed return to sport after first-time patellar dislocation in adolescents: A prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: First-time lateral patellar dislocation is common in adolescent athletes and may cause persistent functional impairment despite nonoperative treatment. Early predictors of delayed return to sport remain incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVE: To identify early clinical and functional factors associated with delayed return to unrestricted preinjury-level sport after first-time lateral patellar dislocation in adolescents.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study included 160 adolescents aged 12-18 years (97 females, 63 males) with first-time traumatic lateral patellar dislocation managed nonoperatively. Participants underwent standardized rehabilitation and were followed for 12 months. At 3 months, quadriceps limb-symmetry index (LSI), single-leg hop performance, Y-Balance asymmetry, patellar apprehension, Banff Patellofemoral Instability Instrument 2.0 (BPII 2.0), and Pediatric International Knee Documentation Committee scores were assessed. Delayed return to sport was defined as failure to resume unrestricted preinjury-level sport within 6 months. Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: Seventy-six participants (47.5%) experienced delayed return to sport. Compared with timely returners, they had lower quadriceps LSI, poorer hop performance, greater Y-Balance asymmetry, more frequent patellar apprehension, and worse patient-reported function. Independent predictors were each 10-percentage-point decrease in quadriceps LSI (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.82, 95% CI 1.29-2.57), persistent patellar apprehension (aOR 2.71, 95% CI 1.31-5.62), and each 10-point decrease in BPII 2.0 score (aOR 1.51, 95% CI 1.13-2.02). The model showed good discrimination (AUC 0.80, 95% CI 0.73-0.86).
CONCLUSION: Reduced quadriceps symmetry, persistent apprehension, and poorer instability-specific function were independently associated with delayed return to sport, supporting multidimensional, criterion-based rehabilitation in adolescents.

title: The combined influence of athletic identity and social support networks on rehabilitation adherence during sports injury recovery: A longitudinal investigation utilizing real-time experience sampling methods.
abstract: This study examined the interactive effects of athletic identity and social support on rehabilitation adherence across recovery phases among injured athletes using experience sampling methodology (ESM). A total of 142 competitive athletes (18-35 years) with moderate‑to‑severe sports injuries requiring 8-12 weeks of rehabilitation were recruited. Athletic identity and perceived social support were measured by validated questionnaires, and adherence was assessed via clinic attendance, home exercise records and therapist ratings. ESM assessments were delivered three times daily over 12 weeks. Mixed‑effects models revealed significant temporal variation in adherence, declining from 76.8% (early phase) to 64.2% (middle phase) and rising slightly to 69.5% (late phase). Athletic identity and social support exhibited a significant interaction. Athletes with high athletic identity and high social support showed 84.2% adherence, while high‑identity athletes with low support only reached 58.6%. Daily perceived social support positively predicted same‑day adherence, with emotional support exerting a stronger effect than instrumental support; the predictive model yielded an AUC of 0.847. Our findings indicate that adherence depends on the joint effect of athletic identity and social support. Clinicians should evaluate athletes' identity profiles and available social support to design tailored rehabilitation adherence interventions.

title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading1,2. High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery3,4. Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery.
DESCRIPTION: The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion.
ALTERNATIVES: Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization5,6. Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern2,7,8.
RATIONALE: This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport8. Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients6,7. Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence.
IMPORTANT TIPS: The small anchor diameter and use of suture tape allow easy access without hardware burden.○ Suture choice depends on surgeon preference regarding construct stiffness and on the tissue quality and risk of irritation. We believe that suture tape lays flatter and, if required, knots are smaller.Avoid suture twisting or kinking, which can prematurely lock anchors, compromising fixation.○ After the anchor is placed, we keep the suture tape secured out of the field as we prepare the capsule with absorbable suture. As we load the second anchor, we maintain tension on the tape to prevent twisting.Overtightening the MTPJ capsule may lead to altered biomechanics.

title: The relationship of grip and three-point pinch strength to ball velocity and elbow varus torque in high school pitchers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hand and forearm strength play an essential role in modulating and controlling forces across the elbow during pitching. In particular, grip and pinch strength reflect functional capacity of the flexor-pronator mass, which contributes to both performance and dynamic stability of the elbow. While diminished grip strength is often used clinically to monitor recovery following shoulder and elbow injury, values in adolescent pitchers are lacking. Furthermore, the relationship between grip and pinch strength with ball velocity and elbow varus torque remains poorly defined.
METHODS: Thirty-eight healthy high school pitchers (16.0 ± 0.9 years, 183.3 ± 6.0 cm, 78.1 ± 9.2 kg) were included in this study. Bilateral grip and three-point pinch strength were assessed prior to pitching. Pitchers were then analyzed using 3D motion capture (480 Hz) and ball velocity was recorded with Trackman throwing fastballs. The pitch with the greatest ball velocity was used in the analysis. Paired t-tests compared dominant and non-dominant grip and pinch strength, and linear regression examined relationships between strength, ball velocity, and elbow torque (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Dominant arm grip strength was greater than the non-dominant throwing arm (P = .001), while pinch strength showed no side to side differences (P = .696). Dominant grip strength demonstrated weak associations with height (r2 = 0.221, P = .002), weight (r2 = 0.217, P = .002), and ball velocity (r2 = 0.116, P = .021). No significant relationships were found between grip strength and elbow varus torque. Pinch strength was not associated with height, weight, age, elbow varus torque, or ball velocity.
DISCUSSION: While forearm musculature is thought to enhance medial elbow stability, grip and pinch strength were not associated with elbow varus torque in high school pitchers. These results suggest that static hand strength measures may not reflect the complex, dynamic demands placed on the elbow during pitching. Further evaluation may be necessary to determine secondary impact such as load and subsequent fatigue on the flexor pronator complex.
CONCLUSION: Grip and pinch strength values in high school pitchers may serve as reference data for clinicians assessing adolescent pitchers. Grip strength demonstrated a weak association with ball velocity; however, neither grip nor pinch strength was significantly related to elbow loading. This highlights the need for future work examining dynamic forearm muscle function in injury risk, recovery, and performance.

title: Objective Return-to-Sport (RTS) Decision Frameworks for Adolescent Shoulder and Elbow Injuries: Tests, Thresholds and Exercise Targets.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent shoulder and elbow injuries are increasing due to sports specialization and year-round training, yet return-to-sport decisions typically rely on adult-derived heuristics that fail to address the unique physiology, growth plate vulnerability, and recovery needs of developing athletes aged 10-19 years.
OBJECTIVE: This review proposes a novel, objective three-pillar RTS framework integrating: (1) foundational tissue capacity, (2) dynamic movement quality and neuromuscular control, and (3) sport-specific load tolerance. We synthesize current evidence to establish provisional, consensus-based adolescent thresholds and provide a practical bedside toolkit for immediate clinical implementation.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative synthesis of contemporary original evidence, consensus recommendations, and validation studies relevant to adolescent shoulder and elbow rehabilitation. Evidence was critically appraised for youth-specific validation, with explicit distinction between evidence-based interventions and emerging aspirational technologies requiring prospective adolescent cohort validation.
RESULTS: We propose a hybrid benchmarking model combining limb symmetry indices (LSI ≥90%) with population-referenced percentiles (≥25th percentile for age/sex/sport) as provisional, consensus-based thresholds. A three-stage progression is outlined: Clinic-ready (pain-free ROM, isometric IR/ER LSI ≥90%), Training-ready (dynamic rotational LSI ≥90%, preserved scapular kinematics), and Game-ready (sport-specific tolerance with 5% velocity loss during simulated exposure). We provide a low-resource bedside toolkit including belt-stabilized hand-held dynamometry, Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test (CKCUEST), Push-Up Plus, Athletic Shoulder positions, seated medicine-ball throw, and simple interval tolerance simulations with specific protocols and thresholds. A stepwise algorithm advances from capacity → movement quality → load tolerance with targeted remediation at each gate.
CONCLUSION: Moving beyond time-based or adult-derived heuristics, this objective multidimensional framework aligns tissue recovery with sport-specific demands through quantifiable metrics. While provisional thresholds require further adolescent validation, the framework offers an evidence-guided pathway that mitigates reinjury risk, restores performance, and supports safe reintegration into sport. Implementation requires adolescent-specific normative databases, stakeholder communication, and cost-effective technological integration for equitable adoption.

title: A rare traumatic triad: Open bicondylar non-conjoint Hoffa fracture with partial tibial tubercle and medial epicondyle avulsions - A case report and biomechanical analysis.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Coronal shear fractures of the distal femoral condyles are rare intra-articular injuries, and the simultaneous occurrence of a non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture with a partial anterior tibial tubercle avulsion and a medial epicondyle avulsion constitutes an exceptionally complex traumatic triad. We report the case of a 35-year-old male motorcyclist who sustained this "floating" articular block injury (AO/OTA 33-B3.3) following a high-velocity accident. Diagnostic assessment utilizing Computed Tomography with 3D reconstruction revealed a vertical Letenneur Type II fracture of the medial condyle and a comminuted Letenneur Type I fracture of the lateral condyle, complicated by significant rotational instability. Surgical management prioritized the posterior femoral instability through a double posterior approach, which allowed for direct visualization and anatomical reduction. Fixation was achieved using posterior-to-anterior headless compression screws, augmented by a posterior buttress plate on the lateral column to neutralize shear forces, while the medial epicondyle was anatomically reduced and fixed; the stable partial tibial tubercle avulsion was treated conservatively. At the two-year follow-up, the patient demonstrated excellent functional recovery with 120 degrees of flexion, a Lysholm score of 91, and a successful return to recreational sports. This case highlights the importance of the double posterior approach and "targeted rigidity" in managing multidirectional instability, permitting early mobilization even in the presence of complex extensor mechanism involvement.
INTRODUCTION: Coronal shear fractures of the distal femoral condyles (Hoffa fractures) are rare intra-articular injuries, with bicondylar patterns being exceptionally uncommon. A non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture combined with a partial anterior tibial tubercle (ATT) avulsion and a medial epicondyle avulsion represents a complex, "floating" articular block that challenges standard treatment algorithms. This case report analyzes the biomechanics and management of this rare traumatic triad.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 35-year-old male motorcyclist presented with a Gustilo-Anderson Type I open knee injury following a high-velocity crash involving hyper-flexion and valgus stress. CT imaging confirmed a non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture (AO/OTA 33-B3.3, Bagaria Type 3). The lateral condyle presented as a Letenneur Type I fracture with extensive comminution, while the medial condyle was a Letenneur Type II vertical fracture. Associated injuries included an Ogden Type I partial ATT avulsion and a Watson-Jones Type I medial epicondyle avulsion.Surgical management utilized a double posterior approach to visualize and reduce the posterior fragments. Fixation involved headless cannulated compression screws for both condyles, augmented by a posterior buttress plate on the lateral column to resist shear forces. The medial epicondyle was refixed with a screw and washer, while the stable ATT avulsion was managed conservatively. At the two-year follow-up, the patient achieved excellent functional outcomes, including 120° of flexion, a Lysholm score of 91, and a Tegner Activity Scale score of 7.
CONCLUSION: Managing this complex triad requires a thorough understanding of the injury mechanism, which involves coronal shear, valgus stress, and eccentric extensor loading. 3D CT reconstruction is mandatory for planning, and a double posterior approach provides superior visualization for anatomical reduction and posterior-to-anterior fixation. Rigid fixation, particularly using anti-glide plating for the lateral column, permits early mobilization and the conservative management of stable associated injuries, leading to high patient satisfaction.

title: Dose-dependent effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation combined with sprint interval training on performance adaptations in basketball players: a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players.
METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]).
RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables.
CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Reduction in Force Complexity Following Eccentric Exercise That Elicits Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Unaccustomed eccentric exercise has been shown to lead to muscle damage. Previous research suggests that fatigue reduces the complexity of muscle force output. However, previous research has not investigated whether the force complexity response to fatigue is affected by eccentric exercise. Therefore, the purpose of the present study was to examine the effect of eccentric exercise and a subsequent fatiguing task on force variability and complexity.
METHODS: Twelve individuals (six females) participated in the study. The participants performed eccentric exercise consisting of six sets of 10 repetitions of the knee extensors to elicit muscle damage. Before and 48 hr after eccentric exercise, the participants were assessed for maximal voluntary contraction and performed a sustained isometric time to task failure protocol at 25% of maximal voluntary contraction. Force variability was assessed in the first 10 s (Fresh) and last 10 s (End-Task) of the time to task failure via standard deviation, coefficient of variation, detrended fluctuation analysis, sample entropy, and multiscale sample entropy.
RESULTS: Maximal voluntary contraction (532.67 ± 177.49 N vs. 448.54 ± 186.92 N, p < .001) and time to task failure (197.10 ± 44.81 s vs. 157.70 ± 62.52 s, p = .031) were reduced after eccentric exercise. There were no differences in force variability following eccentric exercise at either the Fresh or End-Task time points. Force complexity was reduced at both Fresh (detrended fluctuation analysis: 1.37 ± 0.18 vs. 1.47 ± 0.21; sample entropy: 0.88 ± 0.27 vs. 0.71 ± 0.027) and End-Task (sample entropy: 0.63 ± 0.17 vs. 0.53 ± 0.15), following eccentric exercise compared with the pre-eccentric exercise condition.
CONCLUSIONS: Reductions in force complexity, but not force variability, were observed following eccentric exercise. These changes are thought to be due to changes in motor control strategies to compensate for damaged tissue.

title: Imaging of acute sports injuries of the shoulder girdle.
abstract: Acute injuries of the shoulder girdle commonly result from sports activities and lead to imaging studies. Radiologists who interpret these studies should be familiar with traumatic mechanisms and the imaging manifestations of glenohumeral dislocation, acromioclavicular sprain, rotator cuff tear, labral tear, osseous contusion or fracture, and myotendinous strain. Imaging findings are crucial for making accurate diagnoses, grading the severity of injuries, guiding treatment plans, and managing the athletes' expectations for rehabilitation and return to sport. In this review article, we address common and uncommon injuries in both young and mature athletes. Focusing on magnetic resonance imaging, we provide examples of classic injuries and discuss pitfalls that challenge diagnostic interpretation.

title: Effects of muscle length and age on neuromuscular responses to maximal eccentric contractions of the plantar flexors.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Eccentric contractions induce greater neuromuscular impairment and muscle damage than concentric contractions. Muscle length is a key modulator of these responses, yet the combined effects of eccentric contractions and muscle length on neuromuscular function in older adults remain unclear. We investigated acute and delayed neuromuscular responses to eccentric plantar flexor contractions performed at different muscle lengths in young and older adults.
METHODS: Twenty-four young and 26 older adults performed 10 sets of 10 maximal eccentric plantar flexor contractions at either short (30°-0° plantar flexion) or long (0°-30° dorsiflexion) muscle lengths (12 young and 13 older adults per condition). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, voluntary activation, and evoked responses (100 Hz and 10 Hz doublets) were measured before, immediately after, and 1, 24, and 48 h post-exercise. Changes were compared between groups and conditions.
RESULTS: Despite similar torque-time integrals between young and older adults within the same muscle length condition, a muscle length effect was only found in young adults, with a greater (p = 0.021) MVIC decrease at long (-33.6 ± 13.2%) than short lengths (-8.4 ± 15.7%). Older adults showed similar reductions across conditions (≈ - 14-21%). Voluntary activation decreased only at long lengths, with no age difference. Evoked responses showed an age effect (p = 0.032), and the 10/100 Hz ratio decreased only in young after long muscle lengths. Neuromuscular function returned to baseline within 24 h indicating no evidence of severe alteration, although muscle soreness remained elevated at 48 h.
CONCLUSION: Long muscle length eccentric contractions induced greater force loss in young but not older adults, with no evidence of prolonged functional impairment in healthy, physically active older adults.

title: Are both hemolysis and impaired myocyte integrity associated with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
abstract: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is a potent antioxidant enzyme. G6PD deficiency, predominant among males, is a neonatal "neurotoxic" risk, characterized by episodic hemolysis that is sometimes infection triggered. Clinical risk among heterozygous G6PD-deficient females is often under-recognized. Recent reports of rhabdomyolysis among G6PD-deficient individuals are reviewed here. In one case, a male athlete with G6PD deficiency (<10% activity) experienced multiple, acute episodes of rhabdomyolysis, painful muscle symptomatology, injury and hemolysis after strenuous exertion. Both his mother with G6PD-deficiency (<45% activity) and maternal grandmother have chronic histories of episodic or triggered fatigue-related disruptive symptoms. Other case reports of G6PD-deficient individuals with muscle injury and exertional symptoms (with or without hemolysis) showed unique laboratory findings of elevated creatine kinase, myoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, and aminotransferases levels and myoglobinuria. Disrupted myocyte energetics and loss of cellular integrity can be attributed to impaired downstream pentose phosphate pathway (PPP)-related oxidant stress protection, which is a key enzymatic consequence of G6PD-deficiency. These triggered stresses may explain the muscle fatigue and propensity to exertional injury. Correlation between stress-sensitive-impaired muscle injury among all G6PD-deficient individuals, including neonates, requires further clinical validation to ascertain oxidant-stress impact of impaired PPP-dependent cellular energetics of red blood, white blood, neural, and muscle cells.

title: Bilateral erector spinae and biceps femoris co-activation following unilateral hamstring injury in young sprinters.
abstract: This study compared coactivation and strength of the erector spinae (ES) and biceps femoris long head (BFLH) during isometric knee flexion and trunk extension in sprinters with a recent BFLH injury. Twenty-four sprinters with grade 2 BFLH injury and 21 controls performed prone trunk extension and knee flexion maximal voluntary contractions (MVCs) at 90° and 0° knee flexion. Torque and surface electromyography (EMG) of the ES and BFLH were recorded bilaterally and normalized to MVCs during 30° trunk extension and 0° knee flexion, respectively. Previously injured athletes showed a greater co-contraction index (CCI) during knee flexion at 0° and 90° than controls (p < 0.001), with higher ES activation (32.52 ± 17.08 to 47.72 ± 17.83% MVC) than the uninjured group (21.56 ± 14.52 to 44.68 ± 18.02% MVC; p < 0.05). No group differences were found in normalized BFLH EMG, CCI during trunk extension, or absolute knee flexion or trunk extension strength (p > 0.05). Previously injured sprinters showed larger between-limb knee flexion strength asymmetries (>10%, p < 0.01), which were absent in controls. This paraspinal overactivation and increased trunk-hamstring co-contraction after BFLH injury suggest that lumbopelvic control exercises may be beneficial for preventing BFLH re-injury.

title: Gait Retraining for Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome: A Biomechanical Approach to Pain Relief and Performance Optimization.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is common among runners and is linked to biomechanical dysfunctions that increase patellofemoral joint stress. Gait retraining has been proposed to redistribute this loading, but the effectiveness of different retraining strategies and their long-term impact remain unclear. This scoping review synthesizes existing evidence on gait retraining strategies for PFPS, focusing on pain, function, and biomechanics.
DATA SOURCES: MEDLINE, Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus, PEDro, and Web of Science were searched, following the methodological framework of the Joanna Briggs Institute for scoping reviews. Studies investigating gait retraining interventions in runners diagnosed with PFPS were included. Key outcomes were pain reduction, functional improvement, biomechanical adaptations, and adverse effects.
MAIN RESULTS: Three randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria, examining cadence modification, impact reduction, and foot strike adjustments. Intervention groups experienced significant pain reduction, with Visual Analog Scale scores improving by 2 to 4 points, alongside functional gains reflected by increased Kujala and Knee Outcome Survey of the Activities of Daily Living Scale scores. Biomechanical adaptations included decreased patellofemoral joint stress, lower impact forces, and improved load distribution. Some participants reported transient calf discomfort during the adaptation period, which resolved over time.
CONCLUSIONS: Gait retraining is an effective intervention for runners with PFPS, showing sustained pain relief, functional improvement, and biomechanical benefits. Individualized protocols and gradual implementation are essential to optimize outcomes and minimize discomfort. Future research should address long-term retention of gait modifications, optimal training parameters, and applicability beyond runners.
journal: Clinical journal of sport medicine : official journal of the Canadian Academy of Sport Medicine

title: Refining Home-Based Squat Training: The Role of Hip Adduction in Improving Neuromuscular Control for Clinically Diagnosed Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome.
abstract: BACKGROUND Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) often stems from neuromuscular imbalances, particularly vastus medialis obliques (VMO) dysfunction impairing patellar tracking. Research is shifting toward integrated rehabilitation strategies, such as combining hip adduction with squats to enhance VMO recruitment. MATERIAL AND METHODS Thirty participants with PFPS were randomized to traditional squatting (SQU, n=15) or squatting with hip adduction (SQU-HA, n=15) for an 8-week home-based program with identical stretching. SQU-HA squeezed a Swiss ball during squats. Fifteen healthy individuals served as a reference group (RG). Outcome measures assessed before and after intervention included Q-angle, patellar tilt, clinical scales (visual analog scale [VAS], patellofemoral pain severity scale [PSS]), and electromyographic parameters (VMO, vastus lateralis [VL], adductor [ADD] amplitudes, onset times, VMO/VL ratio, and VMO-VL onset difference). RESULTS Both PFPS groups showed significant improvements in VAS and PSS after intervention, with greater VAS improvement in the SQU-HA group (P<0.01). Within-group analysis showed reduced patellar tilt in the SQU-HA group (P=0.003); between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (P=0.217). Muscle activation onset sequences shifted from an abnormal pattern, in which VL activation preceded VMO and ADD activation, to a more typical pattern, in which VMO activation preceded VL and ADD activation. This shift was particularly evident in the SQU-HA group, whose activation pattern resembled that of the RG after intervention. Only VMO-VL onset difference, VMO/VL ratio, and Q-angle were correlated with clinical outcomes (P<0.05). CONCLUSIONS An 8-week SQU-HA program demonstrates promising short-term improvements in VMO-related neuromuscular measures and pain reduction for patients with PFPS. This accessible motor re-education strategy serves as a practical, home-based approach to patellofemoral rehabilitation.
