title: Pes Anserine Bursitis: An Underrecognized Cause of Medial Knee Pain - A Review of Diagnosis, Associated Conditions, and Evidence-Based Management.
abstract: Pes anserine bursitis (PAB) is a frequently underrecognized and misdiagnosed cause of medial knee pain. It occurs when there is inflammation of the bursa interposed between the conjoined pes anserine tendons and the underlying proximal tibia. The purpose of this review is to describe the current knowledge regarding the diagnosis and management of PAB by providing an evidence-based overview of clinical exams and treatment modalities. PAB is prevalent across several high-risk populations, including knee osteoarthritis (OA), obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and athletes engaged in repetitive knee flexion activities. Diagnosis is currently limited by the absence of a validated quantitative clinical assessment tool. The main goal of treatment is to reduce associated bursal inflammation and address the underlying biomechanical and systemic contributing factors. The standard of care is conservative intervention, comprising rest, ice, and short-term NSAID use, then physical therapy and, where symptoms persist, intrabursal corticosteroid injection, with response commonly assessed at eight weeks. Surgery is considered only after these measures have been exhausted. Due to the complexity of overlapping medial knee pathology and the absence of a gold-standard diagnostic method, PAB remains a clinical diagnosis that requires thoughtful history-taking, physical examination, and selective use of imaging. This review summarizes essential clinical examination techniques and treatment options for PAB, emphasizing practical recommendations for orthopedic surgeons. The intended audience also includes sports medicine physicians, rehabilitation specialists, and primary care providers, as most cases are managed conservatively. Referral to orthopedic surgery is appropriate only when symptoms persist despite comprehensive conservative therapy. Although PAB is often diagnosed clinically, structural bursitis is confirmed in only a minority of cases, so management relies primarily on clinical assessment rather than imaging findings.

title: Evolution of Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty: Two Decades of Evidence from the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Reverse shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) has evolved from a salvage procedure to a widely adopted reconstructive solution. This study performed a descriptive bibliometric and content-trend analysis of rTSA publications in the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery (JSES) from 2004-2025.
METHODS: A systematic review identified 506 clinical rTSA studies published in JSES between 2004 and 2025. Extracted variables included publication year, level of evidence, authorship, institution, geographic origin, research topic, demographics, indications, complications, and implant characteristics. Temporal trends were tested using Mann-Kendall trend test and segmented regression; the relationship between implant design representation and complication reporting was evaluated with Spearman rank correlation.
RESULTS: Annual publications increased significantly (BH-adjusted P < .001), peaking at 51 studies in 2023. Mean level of evidence improved (BH-adjusted P < .001), from 4.0 (2006) to 2.86 (2023). Early authorship centered on foundational surgeons (Frankle, Boileau, Walch) and European institutions, later diffusing globally. Mean age rose modestly, though this did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (BH-adjusted P = .077), stabilizing near 70-72 years after 2012. Research focus shifted from complications/technique toward outcomes after 2013, then toward instrumentation, rehabilitation, and cost. Osteoarthritis indications increased (BH-adjusted P = .005) while revision surgery declined (BH-adjusted P = .002). Implant design shifted from medialized to lateralized/non-Grammont configurations (both BH-adjusted P < .001). No individual complication subtype showed a significant temporal trend.
CONCLUSION: RTSA publication trends in JSES reflect the field's evolution from complication-focused study to evidence-driven refinement. Implant design, evidence level, and indications changed significantly, alongside, but not statistically linked to, complication reporting, informing future shoulder reconstruction research directions.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Literature Review, Bibliometric Analysis.
journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery

title: Additive effects of active vitamin D3 or vitamin E administration on therapeutic lower-limb home exercise for knee osteoarthritis: A pilot prospective randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quadriceps weakness, inflammation, and reduced physical function are common in knee osteoarthritis (OA), and lower limb exercise therapy is an established non-pharmacological treatment. Vitamin D3 (vit D3) and vitamin E (vit E) have been proposed as adjunctive therapies; however, clinical findings are inconsistent. We aimed to examine whether combining lower limb home exercises with oral active vit D3 or vit E supplementation provides additive benefits compared with home exercise alone in women with symptomatic knee OA.
METHODS: Eighty-eight postmenopausal women with knee OA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-4; 71.9 ± 5.6 years) were randomly assigned to receive therapeutic lower limb home exercise only, home exercise with active vit D3 administration, or home exercise with vit E administration. Participants performed isometric lower limb exercises twice daily for 24 weeks. Subsequently, they were assessed using the Japanese knee osteoarthritis measure (JKOM) as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were short-form health survey, grip strength, quadriceps muscle strength, 10-m walk test, inflammatory markers, bone mineral density, and body composition. For data analyses, we used paired and independent t tests, analysis of variance, and analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, body mass index, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade.
RESULTS: Eighty participants completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements in JKOM score, quadriceps muscle strength, and 10-m walk test. Grip strength improved significantly only in the group that received active vit D. No significant between-group differences were observed in JKOM scores, short-form health survey-36, muscle strength, or physical performance. Inflammatory markers decreased significantly in the vit E group, although between-group differences were not observed. No other significant between-group differences were found, except in bone mineral density.
CONCLUSIONS: Administering active vit D3 or vit E for 24 weeks as an adjunct to lower limb home exercises did not yield significant additive effects on symptoms, muscle strength, or physical performance in women with knee OA. Exercise therapy alone remained effective, and vitamin supplementation showed nutrient-specific trends.

title: Structured Physiotherapy Improves Functional Outcomes in Acromegalic Arthropathy After Biochemical Remission: A Prospective Controlled Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Musculoskeletal symptoms frequently persist in acromegaly despite biochemical remission, yet the impact of structured physiotherapy on pain, stiffness, and function remains poorly defined.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a standardized knee-focused physiotherapy program in controlled acromegaly and to identify clinical predictors of treatment responsiveness.
METHODS: Thirteen patients with acromegaly in remission and 13 age-, gender-, and BMI-matched individuals with primary knee osteoarthritis completed a 15-session physiotherapy program. Outcomes were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) and WOMAC. Minimal clinically significant difference (MCID) thresholds (≥2 for BPI, ≥10 for WOMAC) determined meaningful improvement. Correlation analyses examined associations between clinical variables and Δ scores.
RESULTS: Acromegaly patients showed significant improvements in all BPI and WOMAC domains (p<0.001). MCID was achieved by 85% for BPI and 100% for WOMAC Total. Pain and function improved most, whereas stiffness showed limited responsiveness. Compared with osteoarthritis controls, acromegaly patients demonstrated smaller Δ changes; baseline-adjusted analyses (ANCOVA) indicated that this attenuated response was largely explained by greater baseline severity in the control group, whereas the persistently greater stiffness in acromegaly remained significant even after adjustment. BMI correlated positively with improvements in BPI Total (r = 0.63) and BPI Pain Severity (r = 0.69), while adenoma size correlated negatively with both measures (r = -0.57 and -0.60). BMI showed a negative association with WOMAC Total improvement (r = -0.59). Stiffness changes were strongly negatively correlated with pretreatment IGF-1 (r = -0.77).
CONCLUSION: Structured physiotherapy yields clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function in acromegaly, while stiffness appears less reversible and more structurally driven. Early musculoskeletal assessment and physiotherapy integration may enhance long-term management.

title: Clinical and functional outcomes of aquatic plyometrics in adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome: a dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Optimal management of adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome requires evidence-based interventions that maximize physical recovery without overloading the patellofemoral joint. This study investigated the efficacy of aquatic plyometric (Aquatic-Plyo) exercises on pain, muscle strength, and functional disability and health-related quality of life in this demographic.
DESIGN: A dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
SUBJECTS/PATIENTS: 56 adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome (age: 10-18 years).
METHODS: Adolescents were allocated to an experimental Aquatic-Plyo group or a control group performing conventional exercises. Both arms completed 45-min sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks. Pre- and post-treatment assessments included pain intensity, isokinetic knee (quadriceps and hamstrings) torque at 120°/s and 180°/s, functional disability, and health-related quality of life.
RESULTS: Mixed-model ANOVA confirmed the therapeutic dominance of the Aquatic-Plyo protocol. It yielded superior pain relief (p = 0.004, η2p = 0.14) and larger increases in quadriceps [120°/s (p = 0.006, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.008, η2p = 0.12)] and hamstring [120°/s (p = 0.007, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09)] peak torque. Moreover, the Aquatic-Plyo intervention drove greater reduction in functional disability (p = 0.03, η2p = 0.08) and notable enhancement in perceived health-related quality of life (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09).
CONCLUSION: Aquatic-Plyo exercises effectively reduces pain and disability while improving muscle strength and health-related quality of life in adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome, making it a valuable addition to conservative rehabilitation strategies.

title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA.
METHODS: This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year.
RESULTS: At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups.
CONCLUSION: The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01939-3.

title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Optimizing Clinical Assessment of Knee Function: Biomechanical Adaptations Across Repeated Single-Leg Hop Trials.
abstract: Single-leg hop performance is widely used in clinics to assess knee function following anterior cruciate ligament injury. However, performance provides limited insight into joint-specific kinetic contributions, and the influence of repeated trials remains unclear. This study quantified the effects of hop directions (forward/vertical/backward) and repeated practice trials on performance and lower-limb joint kinetics. Forty-five injury-free participants performed 10 trials per task. Hop performance and peak moment/power/work at the hip/knee/ankle were calculated. Trials were grouped as one practice attempt and 3 blocks: I (trials 2-4), II (trials 5-7), and III (trials 8-10). Three-by-three repeated-measures analyses of variance were conducted to quantify the effects of task and practice. Backward hop demonstrated the greatest knee moment/work/power and contribution across blocks. Performance increased across blocks in forward and backward hops while remaining consistent in the vertical hop. Knee work was smaller in block I across tasks, whereas backward hop demonstrated greater knee work contribution in block II than in block I. The backward hop places greater knee emphasis, supporting its use as a knee-specific assessment. Minimal practice trials are necessary when using forward/vertical/backward hop performance to assess knee power, whereas at least 4 trials may be required for forward and vertical hops when evaluating knee work.

title: Effects of blood flow restriction training in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) has been proposed as a low-load rehabilitation strategy for symptomatic and postoperative upper-limb musculoskeletal conditions. This review evaluated the clinical effects, tolerability, and prescription characteristics of BFRT in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation.
METHODS: This systematic review was registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420261299726) and reported with reference to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020. CENTRAL/Cochrane Library, Embase via Ovid, MEDLINE/PubMed, Science Citation Index/Web of Science, and Scopus were searched without a start-date restriction before February 18, 2026; backward reference-list/citation checking was also used. Randomized trials, case series, and case reports were eligible. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity, and studies were appraised using risk of bias 2 or design-appropriate Joanna Briggs Institute checklists.
RESULTS: Twenty reports were included: 9 parallel-group randomized trials, 1 randomized crossover trial, 2 case series, and 8 case-report publications. Across the reports, 340 participants were enrolled or randomized and 326 contributed to the analyzed/treated clinical samples; 158 were men (48.5%) and 168 were women (51.5%). In a sham-controlled lateral elbow tendinopathy trial, BFRT resulted in a significantly greater reduction in 12-week pain (between-group difference -1.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.89 to -0.18; P = .026) and patient-rated tennis elbow evaluation (PRTEE) (-15.23, 95% CI -23.57 to -6.90; P < .001). In patients with chronic lateral epicondylitis, PRTEE reduction (-24.20 ± 4.02 vs -15.60 ± 3.71; P = .001) and quick disabilities of the arm, shoulder and hand reduction (-12.83 ± 4.97 vs -7.51 ± 4.72; P = .025) were significantly greater with BFRT plus conventional therapy, whereas between-group pain and strength changes were not significant. In nonoperative distal-radius-fracture rehabilitation, mean activity-pain reduction was 4.0 versus 2.3 points (P = .03). In rotator-cuff tendinopathy, BFRT resulted in significantly greater biceps thickness (P = .002) and internal-rotation strength (P = .040). Conversely, a pragmatic elbow trial found no significant between-group difference in 12-month PRTEE (adjusted contrast + 4.32, 95% CI -9.17 to 17.81; P = .53).
CONCLUSION: BFRT may be considered a low-load adjunct in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation settings, but it is not consistently superior to active rehabilitation for pain, strength, or function. Confidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous prescriptions and co-interventions, uncontrolled designs, and incomplete adverse-event ascertainment.

title: Double-Bundle Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Provides Superior Short-to-Midterm Rotational Stability But Not Clinically Important Functional Gains Over Single-Bundle: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the biomechanical and functional outcomes between single-bundle and double-bundle (DB) anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction techniques using the most current evidence, stratified by follow-up duration.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched from 2013 to September 2025 for randomized controlled trials comparing single-bundle versus DB anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with a minimum follow-up of 24 months. Primary outcomes included anterior tibial translation, rotational stability (pivot shift), and patient-reported outcomes (subjective International Knee Documentation Committee, Lysholm score). Secondary outcomes included return-to-sport and graft failure rate. Continuous outcomes were pooled using inverse-variance random-effects models (DerSimonian-Laird) and dichotomous outcomes using Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect models, with stratification by follow-up duration (24-48 months vs >48 months). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic.
RESULTS: Thirteen randomized controlled trials (1041 patients; 536 single-bundle, 505 DB; mean age 30.2 years; 68% men; follow-up 24-122 months) were included. At 24 to 48 months, DB reconstruction significantly reduced the risk of a positive pivot shift (risk ratio 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.43-0.84, P = .003; number needed to treat = 10) and showed statistically higher subjective International Knee Documentation Committee (mean difference 5.88 points, 95% CI 0.44-11.33) and Lysholm (mean difference 7.47 points, 95% CI 0.06-14.88) scores; however, neither reached established minimal clinically important difference thresholds (11.5 and 8.9 points, respectively). Anterior tibial translation did not differ significantly between techniques (mean difference -0.34 mm, 95% CI -1.04 to 0.35, P = .327). No study reported sex-disaggregated outcomes or individual-level minimal clinically important difference attainment. Beyond 48 months, no significant differences were observed for any outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: DB reconstruction shows statistically significant improvements in rotational stability and patient-reported functional scores at 24 to 48 months, but functional differences do not reach established minimal clinically important difference thresholds. No significant differences were observed beyond 48 months, a finding likely influenced by substantial study heterogeneity and graft selection. The current evidence does not support a universal clinical advantage for the DB technique; shared decision-making based on patient activity demands and surgeon experience remains essential.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

title: Reduced knee adduction moments in bicruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty compared with bicruciate-substituting designs: A contralateral within-patient study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study compared frontal-plane knee loading during gait between bicruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty (BCR-TKA) and bicruciate-substituting TKA (BCS-TKA) using a contralateral within-patient design.
METHODS: Twenty-five patients undergoing simultaneous bilateral TKA received BCR-TKA in one knee and BCS-TKA contralaterally. The final implant selection was determined intraoperatively based primarily on anterior cruciate ligament integrity and functional preservability. Postoperative radiographs were obtained within 1 week before gait analysis, performed 287.4 ± 160.6 days after surgery (range, 109-739 days). The primary outcome was the first peak knee adduction moment (KAM). Secondary outcomes were the second peak KAM and the KAM impulse. Linear mixed-effects models were adjusted for postoperative hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA), joint-line obliquity (JLO), and stance-phase knee varus angle.
RESULTS: Postoperative HKA (3.24 ± 3.1° vs. 3.50 ± 3.4°; P = 0.767) and JLO (178.33 ± 4.8° vs. 178.03 ± 5.0°; P = 0.757) were comparable between BCR-TKA and BCS-TKA. Adjusted first peak KAM was lower with BCR-TKA (BCS-BCR difference, 0.052 Nm/kg; 95% confidence interval, 0.011-0.094; P = 0.014), as was second peak KAM (difference, 0.035 Nm/kg; 95% confidence interval, 0.002-0.068; P = 0.038). KAM impulse did not differ significantly (P = 0.128). All patient-reported outcomes were comparable; Forgotten Joint Score-12 was 24.4 ± 10.7 vs. 25.6 ± 12.0 (P = 0.287).
CONCLUSION: BCR-TKA was associated with lower first and second peak KAMs despite similar postoperative alignment, whereas KAM impulse and patient-reported outcomes were comparable between the implant designs.

title: Creative Solution for Recurrent Failure of Flexor Tendon Repair.
abstract: Flexor tendon injuries present complex surgical and rehabilitative challenges, particularly in zone 2 of the hand. This article presents a case of recurrent flexor tendon failure in a young manual laborer, detailing initial repair, rupture, and secondary reconstruction. Despite multiple complications, including recurrent ruptures and repair failures, the case underscores the importance of individualized surgical planning, coordinated rehabilitation, and shared decision-making in achieving optimal functional recovery.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases.
METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047).
CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol.
METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength.
RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status.
CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

title: Recorded Adverse Events and Patient-Reported Outcomes After Intra-articular Extracellular-Vesicle Product Administration for Knee Osteoarthritis: A Retrospective Single-Practice Case Series.
abstract: Background Exosome-based products are being used for symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (OA), although human efficacy data remain limited and no extracellular vesicle product is approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration for intra-articular use. This study evaluated patient-reported outcomes, subsequent interventions, conversion to total knee arthroplasty (TKA), and recorded adverse events following intra-articular treatment. Objective The aim of the study was to compare pre-injection Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS-JR) scores with scores obtained at six weeks and at the latest follow-up, and to document subsequent conversion to TKA. Study design This retrospective case series provides Level IV evidence. Methods Consecutive intra-articular knee treatments administered between December 2024 and August 2026 were retrospectively reviewed. Patients received either Patient Pure X (PPX™), an autologous platelet-derived extracellular-vesicle preparation, or DayZero™, an allogeneic perinatal tissue-derived extracellular-vesicle preparation manufactured by ZEO ScientifiX. For the primary patient-level analysis, one eligible index knee per patient was included to preserve independence of observations; laterality-ambiguous bilateral KOOS-JR observations were excluded from knee-specific patient-reported outcome analyses. Primary outcomes were paired changes in KOOS-JR from baseline to six weeks and latest follow-up. Secondary outcomes included subsequent nonsurgical interventions, subsequent TKA, and documented administration-related adverse events. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used. Results Fifty-one treated knees in 47 patients were included. Mean age was 75 years (range, 44-94 years); 28 patients were women, and 19 were men. In the primary patient-level analysis, 33 patients had complete, laterality-attributable paired baseline and six-week KOOS-JR data. Mean KOOS-JR increased from 60.0 to 78.5, a mean increase of 18.5 points (95% CI, 13.2-23.8; p<0.001); 30 of 33 patients (90.9%) had higher scores. At the latest follow-up, 36 patients had complete paired data; mean KOOS-JR increased from 60.6 to 77.4, a mean increase of 16.8 points (95% CI, 11.4-22.3; p<0.001), with 30 of 36 patients (83.3%) having higher scores. Three of 47 patients subsequently underwent TKA. No administration-related adverse events were documented in the available practice records; however, adverse-event ascertainment was retrospective. Conclusions In this retrospective single-practice case series, mean KOOS-JR was 18.5 points higher at six weeks than at baseline among 33 patients with complete, laterality-attributable paired data following intra-articular administration of extracellular-vesicle products. Later outcome assessments were limited by nonuniform follow-up and subsequent treatments. Three of 47 patients subsequently underwent TKA. No administration-related adverse events were documented in the available practice records; however, retrospective ascertainment and the limited sample size preclude conclusions regarding safety or tolerability. These descriptive findings do not establish efficacy, clinical importance, comparative effectiveness, structural disease modification, or long-term benefit. Prospective controlled studies using well-characterized products, standardized follow-up, prespecified management of subsequent interventions, and active adverse-event surveillance are warranted.

title: Preoperative subacromial autologous conditioned plasma (ACP) injections and histological and immunohistochemical findings in degenerative supraspinatus tendon tears - results of a prospective comparative cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Degenerative supraspinatus tendon quality is a key determinant of healing after rotator cuff repair, and advanced histological degeneration has been associated with increased retear rates. While platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been extensively studied as an intraoperative adjunct, the potential role of preoperative biological tissue conditioning using platelet-rich plasma remains poorly defined.
HYPOTHESIS/PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the association of preoperative subacromial PRP injections (autologous conditioned plasma, ACP®, Arthrex, Naples, Fl.) with histological and immunohistochemical characteristics of degenerative supraspinatus tendons at the time of rotator cuff repair. It was hypothesized that preoperative ACP treatment would be associated with lower Bonar and degeneration scores compared with untreated controls.
METHODS: A prospective comparative cohort study was performed including patients undergoing arthroscopic repair of isolated, degenerative full-thickness supraspinatus tendon tears. The intervention group received three preoperative subacromial ACP injections (two in one patient) within 3 to 4 weeks before surgery, with the final injection administered no more than 1 week preoperatively. A control group of patients who declined ACP did not receive biological preconditioning. Intraoperatively, tendon biopsies were harvested from the lateral edge of the supraspinatus tendon. The Bonar score and a semiquantitative degeneration score were the co-primary endpoints. Ki-67, CD31 and CD45/LCA immunostaining were exploratory endpoints.
RESULTS: Fifty-four patients were included (ACP group, n = 24, control group, n = 30). The ACP group had lower Bonar scores (6.5 ± 2.0 vs 8.2 ± 1.3, mean difference -1.7, 95% CI -2.7 to -0.7, adjusted P = .044) and lower degeneration scores (1.7 ± 0.8 vs 2.2 ± 0.6, mean difference -0.5, 95% CI -0.9 to -0.1, adjusted P = .044) than controls. CD31 immunostaining was higher in the ACP group, but this difference was not significant after correction for multiple testing (adjusted P = .100). Ki-67, CD45/LCA, reparative changes and the proportion of necrotic tissue did not differ between groups.
CONCLUSION: Preoperative subacromial ACP injections were associated with lower Bonar and degeneration scores in degenerative supraspinatus tendons at the time of rotator cuff repair. The differences were small, the difference in Bonar score was below the predefined minimal clinically important difference, and the clinical relevance of these findings is unclear.
